Now I'm recording.
Okay.
So, I think we should start in Memphis.
Well, in Memphis you want to know how I ran away from home?
Yes. You were born in Memphis?
Born in Memphis, Tennessee. You want me to tell you my age? All right, don't publish it yet. April 1st, 1895. You're not going to publish it yet?
No, no.

Okay. All right. 1895. Well, I went to Auction Street School -- what school I went to. Went to Auction Street School, and my school teacher was getting ready -- a lady had let her child come from Chicago to Memphis. And the lady wouldn't let the child -- let my school teacher bring her back to Chicago. So my school teacher had a pass that this child had come from Chicago to Memphis on. And so she -- I had just been to the store for my mother, and she said, "Well, goodby," -- they called me Pig, you know, "Goodby, Pig, I'm going away. Going back to Chicago." So I said, "I wish I could go." She said, "Well, you can go if your mother says you can go." So I fooled her. I said, well, I'll go home and ask

my mother. I ran up the street, like I was going to ask my mother, and I came back and told her my mother said it was all right, I could go. So she said she was going to get on the train. She told me where to meet her down the street, so I met her down on the street, and we went down to the station. And I had on some blue shoes, some red shoes and a blue dress. And so she took me on into the station, and the man hollared, "All out for the northbound trains."

So Miss Florida -- her name was Florida Cummings -- her middle name -- maiden name was Florida Cummings, but she was married to Mr. Edgerton. So they took me on the train, and when they got on the train the conductor came around to get the tickets, and I was sitting between them. And he said to Miss Florida, "How old is this child?" She said, "She's eight years old." So he passed by; didn't say anything else and kept going.

So I knew a girl in Chicago by the name of Ellen Winston. Her mother and my mother knew each other. So when we got to Chicago, why I got off the streetcar -- we got on the streetcar, and I got off the streetcar on State Street. I know -- in front of a big building called the Burlington Building. Well, I didn't know where I was going, but I knew it was Chicago. So I got off the streetcar and left my schoolteacher and her husband on the car. Only God knows where I was going, but he led me right in front of this Burlington Building.

And when I got to the building -- you know, like when you get off the streetcar, well, I was facing the building. So I walked upstairs in this building. There was a lady washing. Her name was Miss Love. So I said, "Lady, do you know a girl around here by the name of Ellen Winston?" She said, "No, I don't, child. What you doing here, where are you from?" And I said, "Well, I'm looking for Ellen Winston." She said, "Well, I'm asking you where you're from." So I said, "I'm from Memphis." She said, "Memphis?" I said, "yes, ma'am." She said, "Well, there's a girl that lives here by the name of Helen Winston, and this is her Sunday off. She works out in Hyde Park, so this is her Sunday off." So I said, "Well, will you please, ma'am, let me stay here until she comes?" And she said yes.
So when the girl came it was Ellen Winston, my mother's friend's daughter. And she let me stay there.
So how'd you know where to go?
I didn't know where to go. It was just fate. Fate, the hand of God. That's the reason I just have so much faith in God, Chris. It was just the hand of God that led me to this place, you see.

And so when the girl came, she said, "Pig, what in the world are you doing here?" And I said, "I didn't know where you lived, but I knew you were in Chicago." So she said, "Well, just sit down and take your coat off." I had
kept my coat on all the time, you know, waiting for her, even though the lady told me I was welcome. to come

So she said, "I'll take you out where I work." She was second cook up at this place, Hyde Park, you know. So she took me out there where she worked. But she put her dress on me and combed my hair down a little different. And I forget the lady's name -- I wish I could think of her name, she was such a nice lady, at own this Bodin House. So she told her that I was there from Memphis, and could she possibly find a way to give me some kind of little job to do. And the lady gave me the job peeling potatoes. So I peeled the potatoes. Got along well. I stayed there, too. Stayed there until the lady closed the boarding house. And when the lady closed the boarding house -- in the meantime, while I was there, you know what little time I went to school I used to sing at school, and they told me I could sing, you know.

So when the lady closed the boarding house, during that time I was working for her I was going to the different places called -- didn't call them nightclubs, because that was too modern. I don't know what they called them. But anyhow, I would go to each one and ask them -- the way I approached them I guess they used to laugh. I'd say, "Do you want to hire a girl?"
Cabaret?
Yeah, cabarets, you know. And so I

would go to them and they wouldn't bother with me. But finally one night I get a call -- I had been to all the different ones. And Bricktop worked in one, Cora Green worked in one, different ones. And I had been to one place, and finally one night while I was up at this house -- I was at 3210 Dearborn Street at that time, because we had moved over to 3210 Dearborn Street, over to Miss Durham's house. Well, the telephone call came, said, "Tell Alberta Hunter to come down to Archer and State."

And I went down there -- and I had been down there already singing, you know. And I walked into this place I had been -- had a piano player named Bruce. Now that I know music, he was lousy. He was worse than I was. So the owner -- manager of the place, his name was Roy. So Bruce played a song for me, and it was terrible, because I was singing high soprano, you know, and I didn't know anything about contralto or anything like that.

So Roy said to Bruce -- Roy, the manager, said to Bruce, the piano player, said, "Get her out of here, Bruce, she's lousy." So Bruce said, "Oh, Roy, give her a chance." I heard him say, "Give her a chance, Roy, you see she's nothing but a child. So he said, "All right, give her a chance." And I stayed there -- they hired me. Gave me $10.00 a week. And I stayed there --
That wasn't Dago Frank's ?

Wait a minute. That place was Dago Frank's. That was Dago Frank's. (PHONETIC). And that was the very first nightclub, or cabaret, that I worked in, see. And so I stayed there until... that was in the sporting district, you know. So I stayed there until they closed Dago Frank's. See. When they closed Dago Frank's, in the meantime different people had been hearing about me, you see. Because I started off down there singing my little -- singing the songs they had, "All Night Long," and "Where the River Shannon Flows," you know.

And so by that time, different ones had kind of heard there was a pretty good singer down at Dago Frank's. So I went up to the place called Hugh Hoskins (PHONETIC), that was at 32nd and State. Hugh Hoskins. And there was a girl there, no relation, but her name was Zella Hunter, playing piano. And I went to Hugh Hoskins and I started singing the blues. And I sang my little blues that I had picked out on the piano in my hometown in Memphis, you know. I had picked it out with my finger because I don't know one note from the other, even until today I don't know one note from the other.
(Inaudible).

No. So I started singing the blues, and the people used to come to hear me singing the blues, and especially Downhearted Blues. And the girl, Love Austin, heard me. She came and heard me. She was playing at the old
Monogram, one of the little joints there, theater, you know, little funny theater.

And so she heard me singing, so she said to me, one day, "Say, that's a good song." And she said, -- she sent it into Washington, and they had it copywritten. But she was honest enough to copyright it in my name. She could have stolen it from me. She was an honest, good woman, Loveie was. She sent it into Washington and had it copywritten in my name.

But in the meantime, before she sent it in she was talking. So she said, put the music down. And I said, "Well, I don't know any music, so you write the music down," and she wrote it down. And I told her, I said, "Well, you can have the music, then." I gave her the music -- credit for the music. So that's how she got credit for the music. I gave her credit for that music, because I couldn't write it down, and some other person might have taken it and stolen the whole thing from me, see.

So then I was singing "Down-Hearted Blues" and people were coming in. That was where most of the sporting girls and fellows hung out, at Hugh Haskins, 32nd and State. So oh, I made a lot of money there. And I sang the blues and finally I had done all I could do. I had gone as high as I could go at Haskins. So I'm looking for higher fields, now.
So then they asked me, would I come up to the Panama.

I went up to the Panama. That's at 35th and State. Up there was Nellie Carr, Twinkle Davis, Goldie Crosby, Lord have mercy, what's that other girl's name? Another girl and myself. I'll think of her name, because I want her to be in there. And we was the hot shots, upstairs, you know. And the people used to pass off like Brick, Cora Green, Mattie Wright, Nellie Compton and Florence Mills. They'd come upstairs to hear us, because downstairs was the swing, and we were the blues, upstairs. See, they'd come upstairs to hear us sing.

And I would sing the blues. And in there comes Sophie Tucker, and all the big shows from downtown -- the big stars would come up. But they'd come upstairs to hear us. And then I -- well, I became so popular that everybody was trying to get me then, you know. And then I went -- I think I went next door to Frank Peer's Deluxe. And that's where Freddie Keppard was.

Oh, in the meantime, upstairs in the Panama was a piano player named George Hall. He was magnificent. He was wonderful, George Hall. His name was George Hall. And he played some piano. And the musicians used to come up to hear him play piano.

And so then I went next door and I worked with Jimmy Noone's band and Freddie Keppard was there -- on his own but with Jimmy Noone, see. But he was more like the soloist, Freddie Keppard was. So then after I -- the Dreamland kept

after me -- the Dreamland Cafe. Mr. Bottoms -- it was Bill Bottoms who was Joe Lewis' trainer first -- Joe Lewis' dietician, rather. So then I crossed over to Dreamland, and that's where the Lord put his arms around me. Honey, I went from there to everything. I just sang, and sang, and sang. And I used to -- I was slick, you know, because I was making a lot of money. I'd sing softly to the tables so the next table couldn't hear me so I could get that money for the next table.
(Laughter.)
And then I sang, and Lil Hardin was on piano. Baby Dodds was clarinet, I believe.
Drums.
On drums. Sidney Bechet was on clarinet. Joe Oliver was on trumpet. The Minor Brothers were on drums, too.
MINOR Hall?
No, Minor -- two twin brothers. And then Wellington Broad was on bass. And there was another old man on bass, who was he? Daddy somebody.
Not Pops Foster?
Yeah, Pops Foster. Then I'm trying to think of somebody else -- Mae Bradey, sometimes her band would play with me, too.
She played piano, didn't she?
Yeah. She had a band, too. And sometimes her band would play.
Well, I worked there at Dreamland for so long, and I did so well that Mr. Bottoms heard about Louis, Louis Armstrong. Louis was down South, and Bill Bottoms was owner of the place, as I said.
He was a very dapper --
He was so dapper. And what a gentleman. What a gentleman. He sent South and got Louis. And that's when they brought Louis to Dreamland to work with Joe.
To work with Joe, yes.
To work with Joe Oliver.
It was Bottoms and not Joe who sent for him?

Oh, I think Mr. Bottoms was the one, but I won't be too positive about that. But I think it was Bottoms that sent for Louis, and not Joe, although it might have been Joe. But I think Mr. Bottoms was the one, because people had talked to him about Louis so much. Well, I might be wrong, I can't say for sure.

But anyway, they brought Louis up. And that's when I started working with Louis. And I made several records with Louis and Joe under my baby sister's name, Josephine, Josephine Beatty, B-e-a-t-t-y. I made records under her name, because I was -- in the meantime, they sent for me to record for
Paramount. Now, wait a minute, I'm ahead of my story, because I had done notes on some recording already for the Black Swan record. That was Pace and Handy.
You did that before Paramount?
Yeah.
Yes, that's right. You started with Ray's Dreamland Orchestra.
Yes, sir. And I tell you one thing, I recorded just with Fletcher Henderson on piano for Black Swan, too. And William Grant Still was there in Handy's music part, fixing the music.
Now, when you did -- now the first records that (unintelligible) discographies list are "He's a Darn Good Man to Have Hanging Around" and "How Long, Sweet Daddy, How Long."
That's right.
That was with Ray's Dreamland Orchestra?
Uh-huh.
Then you did, around the same time, could even be the same day, you did --
"Bring Back the Joys".
And "Someday, Sweetheart."
I made that with [Mae Gradie?]
No, they think that was done with Fletcher Henderson.
That was. Uh-huh. Sure, because there
was no band with that.
That was, according to this, was done in New York.
Yes, it was done in New York.
In May of 1921, does that sound right?
It sounds right. But I --
(Inaudible). How did you get to New York?
How'd I get to New York?
From Chicago. I mean, what brought you to New York?
From Chicago, let me see. Well -- oh, from Chicago, I'll tell you how I got to Chicago. I had done everything I could do in Chicago, and I'm looking for some higher ground, you know.
It was called the Big Apple in those days, wasn't it?

No, uh-uh. I don't remember. No, it wasn't called the Big Apple. But anyhow, I was working for higher ground, big or little apple. So I said, I'm going to Chicago -- I mean, to New York. I left Chicago -- I'm trying to think. I left Chicago -- I was trying to think of the day. I can't think of the day. But anyhow, I came to New York, I left Chicago on a Wednesday, and I opened on Broadway on a Saturday.
When I came to Chicago I saw Bill Robertson. And Bill Robertson told me to go downtown and ask for --
You mean when you came to New York?

Yeah. Told me to go downtown and ask for Jack Goldberg, and tell Jack Goldberg he sent me. And I went down there. He told me where to go. And I went down there and they asked me what did I want to sing. And I told them, I said, well, I've got a couple of songs I'll sing. I sing, "You've got to Reap what you Sow," and "If you Want to Keep your Daddy Home."

And they had a piano player. In the meantime, this Bill Vodery, he was -- soon as I got there, I guess I was young and he was looking at me, you know. So he --
He's the one who had the military band?
No, James Reese Europe (PHONETIC) had the military band.
Vodery, didn't Vodery have --

Vodery, I don't remember him having.

But anyway, Bill Vodery, he looked at me in the eye, smiling and going on, so I laid him out in the meantime before I went on the stage because, you know. So he -- I told him -- and meantime, there was a fellow on violin named Will Tyler, marvelous violinist. And he heard me tell Bill Vodery to play choruses, no verse, just to play short introduction, four bar introduction, and two choruses of my first song. And just to play four bars and two bars of the next song. Instead he was going with eight bars.

Well, Vodery had -- Tyler had heard me, what I said, and while Vodery was playing on this introduction, Will Tyler was playing what I had asked him to play, and I went on and sang what I had asked him to play, you know. And so anyhow, in the meantime, they told me to come back. Now, Will Vodery is going to still do that same trick on me my opening night. The night I'm supposed to open will still play eight bars, and Tyler, the violinist, was going to help me and play the four bars like I told him.

So my opening night I started -- I got out on the stage and I started with my first song, with my four bars, because I'm always, you know -- I know what I'm doing. I sang my four bars and Will Tyler was right with me on each one of my songs. And I didn't know stopping the show meant I was doing great. I thought I had wrecked the show -- messed up, you know.

But anyhow, honey, the people were standing, applauding and applauding and carrying on. And when I came off the stage, most of the big celebrities was back there to greet me. And this man, what was his name -- oh, I got to think of this man's name -- said that regardless of a hostile orchestra that I was the only person that ever stood flatfoot and made blues a song. Yes, he did. Listen, you try to find out one of those mean critics. Martin Dale -- Gale, Martin Gale. I'll find -- I'll think of his name.
He wrote this on --

He wrote that in the paper. He said, regardless of a hostile orchestra, that I was the only one -- only person that ever stood flatfoot and made blues a song. Because I never did do all this going around. I used to stand there with my hand on my hip and sing what I wanted to sing, you know. Because I've always tried to make it -- make an effort to have good diction. Because I know it's so important.
So then, after that opening night I had nothing to do but keep going. I sailed, you know. And from that -- that was the show, "How Come."
The Eddie Hunter Show.
Eddie Hunter Show, "How Come." See --
That was what year, now, "How Come"?
I believe that was in '34.
No, that had to have been --
Before that?
Oh, sure, because that was the show Bessie had been in briefly.
Yes. And they couldn't do anything with her.
Yes. This would have had to have been very early twenties.
Well, that was it. Anyhow --
I have all that. I have all the
dates on that, on the "How Come". But that was -- you were talking about when you first came to New York.
Yeah. Well, anyhow --
Around the time when you made these records for Black Swan.
Yeah.
Then when you did "How Come", it must have been around the same time. Sidney Bechet was in that.
Yes, Sidney Bechet.
And he played "How Come".
He did?
He was -- about a Chinese man, right, "How Come"?
Yeah, oh, sure, Bechet was. Yes, made up as a Chinaman.
And that was at the Apollo on 42nd Street.
42nd Street. We're the first group down there, you know, on Broadway. We called it 42nd and Broadway, you see.
That was the first stage show you did.
First stage show, yes.
What did you do in that?
Oh, let me see. Yeah, the first -- I
(Inaudible).
Uh-huh. Did I do anything in that show? I don't remember. I have to think way back.
You went on tour with that show, didn't you?

Oh, yeah. We toured the -- like Baltimore and all those. Then after I came back from the show, I toured by myself, just with a pianist and a dancer. The girl that played piano for -- no, that was before Pearl's time. A girl named Laura played piano for me. And Leroy Bloomfield was my dancer. And we played all the different houses, Washington, Baltimore, and all down that way. And then I got work in the big White Theaters. Like the Keith Houses, and all.
Keith circuit?

Keith circuit. But you see, I had to dress up like -- kind of like gingham apron things, because they wouldn't accept us Negro girls in smart clothes, you know. That's why Ethel Waters made up like that, a washer woman and things. We had to wear clothes, until finally, along toward the last -- of course, this is later, so I won't talk about that.

But anyhow, I toured with an old apron on, and things like that. And Leroy had on overalls. And Laura had on just a plain, little old ordinary something. They wouldn't let us come out there on big time.
performers
How did you and the other black$ -- how did you feel about that, at that time?

Well, of course we resented it, but we wanted to get on big time. So when you want to do something, you accept what you can get until you're in a position to speak out. So we didn't think it was fair, because most of the white girls would come and ask us how we did such and such a thing, you understand. And then several places -- theaters I went, they had me on the stage just -- they'd always put us on second, see, to liven things up for the rest of them.

But, oh, Lord, I have it written down some place, one of the white performers refused to follow me. She said she couldn't follow me. So they had to take me off of second. She refused to follow me. Because instead of making it hot for her, I made it too hot. So they took me off. I have all that down, I think, in a book. And they -- this girl refused to follow me. So now what else?
The reason you used your sister's Josephine Beatty was because you were under name, (inaudible) contract?
To Paramount. So you used it when you did Sennett, for instance?
Yes, when I used Josephine Beatty's name I was under contract for Paramount. That's why I used her name.
Let's see, now, who were you singing --

Beatty
Tod -- Bailey and Todd?
Oh, Mr. Todd, yes.
Tell me about Buster Todd.
Yeah, what was his name? Mr. Todd. Now, he wrote a song, what was his song. You put the name of his song down there?
You did "Cakewalking Babies" with him.
Yeah, I did "Cakewalking Babies" with (unintelligible). Wait a minute, what's that other song? His song, what was his song?
We can find that. (inaudible).
Yeah. Well, I know Mr. Todd. Yeah, I did that with him. And somebody else. I was trying to think --
You recorded with Clarence Williams Blue Five too (inaudible).
"Cakewalking Babies", what was that -- Jack Palmer's song. It will have to come to me later. I can't think of that.
"Nobody Knows the Way I Feel this Morning" (inaudible). Was around that time, too.
Yeah, uh-huh.
But I remember the Gennett record, Beatty Bailey and Todd.
Yes, indeed.
Wasn't it Louie and Sidney Bechet and Clarence Williams?
Clarence Williams, Sidney Bechet, and Louis Armstrong. And who was on guitar? Wasn't somebody on guitar with me?
I don't remember. I have all that information.
You got all information. Uh-huh.
But how did -- did you work with Mr. Todd outside of this --
No.
Just recordings.
Well, Mr. Todd was in a show, I think. I think Mr. Todd was in "How Come" with us.
Oh, was he?

Mr. Carter was in it, because they had a quartet in "How Come." And Mr. Todd was in that quartet. A beautiful quartet. Yes, he was in that show. Mr. Todd, I'm trying -- I don't know, I don't know who else -- who the other singers were. But Mr. Todd -- there was a quartet, and he was -- because they were like the waiters. Because "How Come" was a show -- Eddie Hunter was a marvelous comedian, one of those intelligent comedians, you know. Funny, but -- and he had whiskey would be brown sugar would be whiskey. And gin would be

-- what did they call it? Milk. Milk and sugar, I think. But anyhow, I'll look all that up and tell you about it, hear? And they had -- you'd sit on the bottles, like they were seats for you. And the police would come, we'd run and sit down on those bottles.
That was in the show?

Yeah, that was in the show. And when the cops would leave -- the police were in the show, you know. When they'd leave, why they'd come in and 'Give me a brown sugar', they'd give them the whiskey, see. And that's where -- gin, give them the white stuff. We'd be sitting on the bottles when the cops would come.
That was a wonderful show. And dancing, ooh, ooh.
So during the twenties you were in New York most of the time?
Uh-huh.
Where'd you live in New York?

I lived, yes, one while I lived at 233 West 136th Street. And that was Bert Williams' niece. His oldest niece and I lived there. We had the apartment. And let me see, where else did I live? Oh, 287 Edgecomb, 287 Edgecomb, we had a --
That was a nice area?
Yeah, I had an apartment right over the Morningside -- right over that big park right --
Yeah.
We lived right there. And then I finally --
What was it like in New York?
Oh, New York was wonderful. Oh, and that's when we had the Sugar Hill, you know. And we had the [39th] Striver's Row. 39th Street was Striver's Row, and Sugar Hill was up a little higher.
Was Madam Walker still around?

Madam Walker was one of my best friends. I used to go to her house every Sunday. Wasn't a Sunday I didn't -- didn't miss a Sunday. Lottie Tyler, who was my girl friend, Lottie Tyler and Edna Thomas and let me see, who else, we were considered the dicties, they called us dicties, you know. We were supposed to be the society of New York. Edna Thomas and Henry Branham, Jimmy Daniels -- no, that was before Jimmy's time. No, it wasn't. Jimmy used to go there. Jimmy Daniels, oh what is that boy's name? He's in Hawaii now.
Grand house, wasn't it over there?
Yes, oh, yes. But that was right on St. Nicholas Avenue. 280 St. Nicholas Avenue. Right there between 138th and 39th, on St. Nicholas.
Did she like show business --
All her friends were mostly show people.
They were?
Yeah, she hung out with show people.
In fact, whenever the society people would have the little concerts and things, she would always sing something, Lili Walker would.
She sang?

Yeah. She couldn't -- and then she didn't do too bad at that. She sang -- she would sing a song, always, Lili Walker. And let me see now, what else? So, I've done my vaudeville now -- I mean my show and vaudeville in New York, haven't I?
Yeah, I was just wondering -- I wanted to sidestep a minute about New York, and talk about sort of what life was like in New York at that time for blacks, entertainers, you know.

Well, the entertainers were very popular. And the people in New York, they had their society group too, you know, and some of those entertainers you couldn't afford to associate with, you know. But I was one of the dicties' entertainers, me and --
Bessie, I guess?
No, Lord, Bessie Smith, they wouldn't think of looking at Bessie. Bessie was too raucous, like, you know. Although she was a good singer. But they wouldn't care how good you were --
Background?
It's your background, uh-huh. Although
my background was poor, but it was humble, you know. But Bessie, her's was a little too fantastic.

And let me see, now, in New York you could -- and then there was more home entertainment, too. People would entertain and go to each other's homes, you know, for parties. They'd have parties, oh, my goodness, every week or so somebody would have a party. And well, you want to know how domestically things were? The cooks and things were making good money, and those cooks belong in society, too, you know. They didn't care if they were cooks and janitors. They belonged with the better people.
And then there was --
How about Pullman porters?
(Inaudible).
Yeah, there were Pullman porters had the best dough, because they worked on the road and they had those permanent jobs, and most of the women were married to pullman porters.
They were a good catch, right?

Oh, the best in the world. They were goldfish. Most of them were married to Pullman porters. And there was a fellow that was very much in society, lived at 139th Street, what was that fellow's name? I must ask somebody, because he played for most of the social group -- white people, for the society of New York, Philadelphia, everywhere. He'd go everywhere.
Pianist?

Yeah. Had a band. Had a band, but he'd go as a pianist, too. And then there was -- let me see, did I buy my place on 138th Street? Yes. When I left 287 Edgecomb I bought my place on 138th Street, 133 West 138th Street.
Bought a house there?

One of the first to buy on 138th Street. And I used to -- I was still going around with the society, you know. Then I started working in -- after I had left my nightclubs and things around here, I worked downtown in the nightclubs. I worked down at the Heartbeat Club.
Where was that?
That was down in the Village. One of them early places down in the Village. It was run by gangsters.
This, of course, is during Prohibition?

No, I've come way too far. Because World War I, I was at Dreamland. I remember now, World War I, I had crossed over from the Deluxe and I worked at Dreamland Cafe. Because I remember that they told him he could sell drinks, and not have entertainment. But if he had soft drinks, he could have entertainment. And he kept the soft drinks, and kept us entertainers. That was the Dreamland.
But did they sell the strong stuff?
People brought their stuff.
They brought it, huh?
People brought their own. Now, that was during World War I. So I'm way ahead of my story, aren't I?
That's all right.
Anyhow, during World War I, and then after World War I, that's when I got myself together. And came on to New York. But in the meantime --
That's when prohibition was in?

That's right. In the meantime, when I was at Dreamland, even though I was working at Dreamland, I'd go into a little nightclub, after-hour place downtown -- I mean, down on State Street. And I think that was called the -- I'll ask somebody. Somebody will tell me. Have you got any of those nightclub places -- after hour places? Did I tell you any when I was --
Probably --

$600.00. Johnny Kerry. He had the Nest, you know the Nest Club? He was one of the proprietors of the Nest, he and Mal Fraser had the Nest. And Johnny, I think he was doing booking, too, you know.

Any how, he booked me into John Gibson's Standard Theater and got me $600.00. A week.
That was a lot of money.
Lot of money then, sure was.
You were a headliner.
Oh, yes. Each place I went I was the headliner.
Now were you singing blues then, or were you combining --
Combining them with everything. But I always sang the blues. I always sang the blues. But I was booked in, more or less, for my blues. Because those people at that time were blues crazy. You know.
Yes. I suppose a lot of people would come up -- from the South.

That's right, they sure would. And I'd sing blues. And from there I went into the Dunbar, that was John Gibson's other theater. And then I went to Washington, Howard and Washington. And I went to Baltimore.
When you were going to these various
theaters, you didn't have an agent, did you? A booking agent or manager, something like that?

Most of the time I did it myself. But sometimes some agent would ask me if I would -- but I didn't bother much with the agents. I'll tell you why, because agents they kind of knocked down on you, you know. We called it when they Steal from you, knock down. So I didn't bother much. Most of the time, like if I was in a theater, like I'm in the Howard, somebody would come and say will you go to such and such a theater?
So one thing led to another??

Yeah, uh-huh. And let me see, I was on the bill with Buck and Bubbles and some big name I was on several times. No, that was before Sammy Davis, because I know Sammy, when Sammy was a little boy, he and his uncle, Will Masten and them --
What about Sammy Davis, Senior?

That's what I'm talking about, his uncle, his father, I mean. Will Masten was supposed to be the uncle no more relative than I am. But anyhow -- but Sammy Senior, that was the Will MASTEN trio. That was Sammy, Will, and his father -- SAMmy's father, see.
Now, we worked together in -- wait a minute.
That must have been much later. That's in the 30's.
Yes, uh-huh.
But then when you --
I worked at a place called the Bali in Washington. That was during World War -- was that World War I? Yeah, World War I, wasn't it. Because they had the thing out, the war bonds. Sold war bonds.
They had that in World War II.
Was that World War II? No, honey.
But they may also have had it in World War I. I don't know. But I know they had war bonds in --
But these were war bonds. The World War II didn't say war bonds. It said something else.
Yes.
Didn't it?
War bonds, and then they changed it to defense bonds.
Well, I know in Washington, I got pictures. I'll show you those pictures, in Bali. I headlined all over there.
Did you like -- since you didn't have a manager and agent, did you then negotiate the fee with whoever --

I tell you, sometimes -- now, there was a fellow in Washington, I think I have his picture and his name. He was the one that booked me into the Bali in Washington. And then, as I say, Johnny Kerry booked me into Gibson's in Philadelphia. And also the -- who booked me into the Howard? Mr.

Mann, the man who owned the Howard. And the -- what was that man's name? The man that owned the place would talk to me, he'd talk to me about the contracts. Uh-huh. Very seldom through a booking agent. Uh-huh. Only Mr. GlaSer. Things I got through Mr. GlaSer were the big things, like, you know. Not the little houses in Philadelphia, and all.
Would white people come to Gibson's Standard Theater?

Yeah, you could hardly get in any of those theaters for the white people. Yeah, most of the time it was no place for the colored ones. And especially -- that's another thing about Chicago, you couldn't get in those places for the white people -- in the after hour places, especially. See. No, you could hardly get in them. And Dreamland, of course Dreamland and the Panama and Hoskins -- of course, Hoskins was just about the size of this. Yeah. But the people would come and stand, and take their drinks up off the bar, to hear you sing.
What was the fanciest club in Chicago?
Dreamland.
Dreamland?

Dreamland was the fanciest. It was the biggest and the fanciest. The Sunset was all right. It was all right, but it wasn't as big as the Dreamland, and it wasn't as fancy as the Dreamland. Because Dreamland had all that
glass floor stuff and all, you know.
Sounds pretty fancy.
Yeah, it was pretty fancy. But the Sunset was -- now listen, I tell you one thing, in 1929 -- in 1929 I know I went to work at the with Earl Hines. At the Grand Terrace. I'm sure.
Now, '29 was the year --
I had been to Europe. I had been to Europe and I came back. And when I came back I went out there and then did a few weeks with Earl Hines.
And then what? Did you go back to Europe?
Yeah.
Oh, I see.
I kept going back and forth. Uh-huh.
So you did -- well, we haven't got to that, yet.
No.
You did "Showboat" in London with Paul Robeson.
That was in '29, you know.
Then you came back and then you went to France and all over the place.
Uh-huh, yeah.
But the clubs -- so the clubs were pretty fancy, but was the Dreamland fancier than anything here
in New York?
Well, you see Dreamland -- I didn't go to any of the clubs downtown at that time.
You went to the small --
Yeah, yeah. Oh, you mean here in --
Barron Wilkins...? (Inaudible)
Oh, you mean was it fancier than these clubs in New York?
Yeah.
Oh, Lord, yes. These clubs in New York haven't got a chance with what the Dreamland was. Only the Cotton Club. And the Cotton Club was more -- no, it didn't compare with Dreamland.
The Cotton Club was for whites only.

Well, a few colored. They used to kind of segregate you at the Cotton Club. Colored people used to kind of get back in the back seats a little bit. They gracefully would find a place to seat the colored people, you know, in the back. But the colored people went just the same. That's when Lena Horne -- they took little Lena up there, you know. She was a kid. Her mother and I were in our first Broadway show together, you know. Lena Horne's mother, Edna.
So let me see, now. No, Dreamland had all of them sewed up for fanciness. Yeah. And Connie's Inn, I worked at Connie's Inn, too.
The uptown -- Harlem Connie's Inn?
I worked at uptown Connie's Inn. And then I came back from Europe and worked at Connie's Inn, you know, 47th and Broadway, where there's a square.
Yes.
Well, I was headlined on each corner.
That became the Latin Quarter later on?
That's right. I was headlined on each -- all four places, the Seventh Avenue, the Broadway -- Seventh Avenue and Broadway.
What was that like? That was Connie Immerman (PHONETIC), right?
Connie Immerman, that's right. Now there's -- Louie was there, too.
Right.
And Louis Russell played there, too.
Bessie played there in '36.
She did? Oh, that's one on me. I didn't know she was there, uh-uh.
They had Billie Holiday there then. And she had -- she got ptomaine poisoning. They brought --
Oh, brought Bessie in.
And Nat Nazzaro.
Oh. He was the one booked Buck and Bubbles.
He brought Bessie in.
He brought Bessie in. Well, I was in Europe at the time, I guess. Uh-huh. Well, did she do all right there?
She stayed -- she was held over for 12 weeks.

Oh, that's good. She must have done all right. Isn't that wonderful. She could -- that woman, you could hear that woman from here to -- at least to Harlem. She had one of the most -- one of the biggest voices I ever -- well, of course Ella Fitzgerald has the truest voice I've ever heard. Her voice is one of the truest I've ever heard. You know, she made an album of 'Downhearted Blues,' and all.
Who did?
Ella Fitzgerald.
Oh, yes, yes.
Yeah. So I guess --
Well, did you -- there were two sort of classes of show business people?
Uh-huh.
The one that Bessie would be around with, and the one that you'd be around with?
That's right.
But wouldn't it sometimes come together?
Did you, for instance, know Carlton Van Vechten?
Oh, very well. Carlton Van Vechten always stopped at my mother's house in Chicago.
Because Bessie --
Carlton Van Vechten
-- got to know Carlton Van Vechten. He liked her.
He liked both of us. He liked both.
(Inaudible).

Yeah, Carlton Van Vechten, Jimmy Daniels, Lilya Walker, Henry Branham, those were the people that Carl came around. That was the big -- supposed to be the high class ones. See, high class people. But now he -- Carlton Van Vechten liked both. He liked Bessie for her lowness, although he was a fine guy, and his wife was just as sweet, you know. They were fine people. But he liked both. He didn't try to, you know, make one feel bad. But we never associated with Bessie, although she was human. But she was just a little rough -- I can't stand a rough woman.
But it was strange, because Porter Granger was a very elegant --
He was very -- always with his walking cane.
I know. And spats.
That's right.
Now he was with Bessie. That must have been a strange combination.
And he worked with me.
Oh, yes.

He worked with me. But he always tried to get Bessie to be a lady. Always. He always used to try to talk to Bessie. He'd take and tell Bessie, Bessie, don't be rough, don't be loud. Because he was such a gentleman. And he never got recognition for the things he did. Now, Porter Granger wrote, 'Michigan Water Tastes Like Sherry Wine.' I recorded that for him. Have you got that?
I have several recordings of that.
Good. Well, I made that with him. And so many things that he didn't get credit for.
He wrote whole shows, didn't he?
Yes, he did.
Did he eventually become mentally ill?
Not that I know of.
How did he --
Well, I think so. But you see, I stayed in Europe most of the time.
That's right.
Uh-huh. But I don't think he was given the credit that he was due.
So you went -- do you remember Sam Wooding?
Yeah, sure. But I didn't -- I never worked with Sam Wooding. I don't remember having worked with Sam Wooding.
He had a nice band.
He had a wonderful band. And oh, just so recognized. Now, he was -- there's another gentleman.
And he still is.
He's a gentleman, what a gentleman. Fine fellow.
Do you see him now?
I don't see him now. I understand he's in America, though.
Oh, sure. He lives right -- he comes over here very often.
He does? Well, you must give him my best regards.
I sure will.
He's a fine fellow. Have we finished?
No, but we're getting there.
All right. You tell me.
(Inaudible) So -- but your everyday life -- you worked late, singing here in New York in the twenties.
Uh-huh.
You'd work in the cabarets or theaters, where ever, late. And then I guess most show business people
went and partied the rest of the night. Or a lot of people.
Well, I didn't. I never did.
You told me once that --
No, I never did. I'd go home, get my sleep, and the time come to go to work, I've never been late on a job in my life. I've been at the hospital 20 years, and I've never been late once.
You had no -- I mean, what did you do then, during the day?
Stay at my mother's.
Uh-huh.
Stay there with my mother, maybe trying to sit in my room and read. I'd read. Used to read a lot.
Well, today, you know, show business people are constantly -- well, they're being interviewed. Was anybody interviewing anybody in those days?
No. I don't remember. I don't remember anybody. Let me see -- yes, a couple of times some fellows tried to interview me, but I found they were Communists, and I never would talk with them.
Oh, they were Communists?
Uh-huh.
Then that was later on.
No, this was --
In the twenties?

Pretty early. They started out early, some of them, you know. But they started out in a different way. You had to be slick enough to know what they were up to. When they started panning my government, then I wouldn't -- I knew they were wrong. That was before they had put anything down.
What about -- now, was it important to you, for instance, to read "The Defender" every week?
Oh, I never missed. Oh, my goodness, I couldn't get to the stand quick enough to get the "Chicago Defender," the New York "Age", that was an old paper then, New York "Age", the --
"The Amsterdam News"?
No, "Amsterdam News" wasn't out then, I don't think.
How about the "Innerstate Tattler"?

Oh, by all means, the "Tattler", and the Pittsburgh "Courier". Oh, I got an article that was -- the fellow put in the Pittsburgh "Courier" about me, the most beautiful article you ever read. And I was always interviewed by those newspapers.
Do you remember Alan McMillan?
Oh, he's here now.
I know.
Yeah, Alan, he did some work for me, too.
Did a lot of work for me. He's --
This was the way -- through these papers -- that you would find out what your colleagues were doing and --

Oh, yes. We couldn't get to the newsstand quick enough to get those papers. The "Amsterdam", the Baltimore paper, the "Tattler", the -- as I said, the New York "Age", the "Afro-American". What beautiful articles they used to always write about me.
The Philadelphia "Tribune"?
"Tribune", all those papers. I mean, all those fellows, they would always put something nice in about me. I don't know why.
Because you're so nice.
Well, thank you. Thank you, Chris. But they'd always say such nice things about me being a lady, and this and the other.
You are.
I always try to be, God knows. I hope I did my mother and grandmother -- hope I did them justice.
What about the white papers now?
The white papers?
Did you ever read them? Were they important to you?
Yes. Yes, the white papers were
important to me, because I always wanted to know what was going on. And I --
(Inaudible). In the world, in general.

In the world, in general. And I always wanted to be able to speak intelligently when I spoke, you know. And then not having a college education, and all, I used to read books. You'd be surprised what the newspapers can do for you if you read them. You know, For instance Frances -- a lot of the girls that have college educations, their grammar is very bad.

But let me ask, now, you were one of the celebrities of the twenties. If you walked into, for instance, Small's in the twenties, did people recognize -- I'm not talking about show business people, now, the other --
Other people recognized me. But not so much the show people.
Did they ever ask for autographs and things?
Oh, yes. Oh, Lord, yes.

The tigers or leopard?

Zebra?
Zebra. She had it trimmed, the rug on the floor of the car was like a --
Zebra skin?
Zebra skin, yeah. And then I -- if I'm

To match the car.
(Laughter)
That's very grand.

I don't recall.
I don't recall. I don't want to say she did.

No, I don't think she smoked.
Oh, yes, she did, because I remember -- I remember her with her white hair and a cigarette dangling from her mouth, --
That's right. That's right.
-- sitting at the piano that morning.
She did smoke.
And we went out and --
And if I'm not mistaken, she always kept
a pack of cigarettes laying on the side of the seat by her.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh, yes, she did smoke. But I -- she didn't drink, I don't think. I don't think Lovie drank.
No, not to my knowledge.
If she did, to my knowledge, in fact, I never saw her drink. If she did, in fact, I don't think she did --

Monogram --
Small theater, wasn't it?

Yeah, very small but packed to capacity at all times, and they did nine and ten shows, and each house was packed. And the people would come out and she'd start the numbers, and she'd start playing and never missed a note, you know, and -- let me see, did Lovie -- not only the Monogram. Didn't she play someplace else?
She was also the music director, I think, at the Paramount --
At the Grand, wasn't she?
-- Paramount records.
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- the house band there.
But this was long -- this was before.
Oh, you're talking about before the '20's.

No, this was the -- the Monogram was the '20's. But I don't remember whether she directed my -- no, she didn't direct my recordings, because they always sent me to New York, to the New York recording laboratory.
Oh, you --
Uh-huh, they would send me from Chicago to New York each time. If I'm not mistaken now, maybe I did -- I don't remember having recorded in Chicago, but maybe I did.
Well, most of yours, you did one with Lovie Austin and Jimmy O'Brian in 1923 --
I did?
Miss Anna Brown and Maybe Someday.
Ye-e-s.

That was mine. I wrote that.
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- Blues -- yeah?
'Experience Blues', that's mine.
So you did those in Chicago.
In Chicago.
And the rest all seem to be done in New York.
In New York because --
That was with Lovie, and I noticed on the -- one of the Lovie's that you're on, Tommy Ladnier --
That's another thing I thought about when I was home. Tommy Ladnier did another recording with me.
Yes, now, wasn't Tommy Ladnier, they were very close, weren't they?
Very, yes.
Lovie and Tom -- because I remember Lovie talking about him.
Yes, they were extremely close, very good friends.
Uh-huh. And he went, of course, with Sam Wooding, in 1925 to Europe.
That's right, to Europe, uh-huh. He was -- he became very popular in Europe too, Tommy did.
Yes. But you made some recordings. Let's see. I'm going to skip to 1929 now. You -- you did for Columbia, you did My Particular Man and Give me All the Love You Got.1)
Well, you're going to skip the other --
the other things that I made before that? You're coming back to it.

Yes. Yes, that was Fats. I did those for Columbia, huh?

Oh, yes, I see.

Uh-huh. Those were good songs, but a couple of them were kind of on the suggestive side, I think.

I didn't.
No.
No. That's --

Mayo, sure.

Of course, Mayo Williams (inaudible).
Mayo Williams was a thief.
I know. I met him.
He was the one.
Right.

But in the meantime Mayo Williams had gotten with Mr. -- not with Mr. Supper -- but I think he had gone to Mills and them -- Mills Music -- and I don't know what he did, but I think he maneuvered a little bit and got some of my money. See?
Yes, that was his way.

That was his way. But Mr. Supper was an honest man. He never cheated me out of a dime. And -- but the contract, you see, the contracts, you got $75.00 a side. And your contract was a fourth of a penny -- I think I've got some -- royalties.

On -- on my compositions, on the records and everything. It all included -- it was inclusive.
I see.
See, the records and the song and all, that fourth of a penny. For instance, if a record sold, whether it was my song on it or not, I only got a fourth of a penny. See?
Uh-huh. So you were getting, actually getting royalties. Did you get it?

Well, I got $368.00, I remember very well. That's the only thing I ever remember getting, from all that money they made, until I finally went to Mills, and the copyright came due, and I beat them to the punch. I got my copyright. See? -- Eubie Blake --
-- Eubie, yes, Eubie, but most of my --

Yes?
Yes.

No.

I see. Huh.

Oh, he did?
Uh-huh.

That came out, uh-huh.

Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah, who was that with there?
That was Fletcher on piano. That was Fletcher.
Well, what is this? What --

Excuse me, but did I tell you that I worked with Tony Jackson, a fellow that wrote 'Pretty Baby'?
No, you didn't tell me that.
I did, in Chicago.
Oh, you did?
Yeah, at the Elkin Number Two.
And this was before you came to New York the first time?
Yeah.
So this was in --
In the '20's.
The '20's, the early -- very early '20's.
Yeah, Tony Jackson.

What about -- now, I notice, for instance, back in '23, which was also the year Bessie started recording, you were doing a lot of the same numbers, "'Tain't Nobody's Business, Aggravatin' Papa, "Bleeding Hearted Blues" --
Quite a big number for me, that was.
"Bleeding Hearted?"
Yes, tremendous.
But you're doing them for Paramount, and she's doing the same songs for Columbia, you know.
Uh-huh.
They were -- must have been sort of rivalry there.
Yeah, rivalry, uh-huh. Maybe that's why she didn't like me.
She didn't -- Bessie didn't like --

I don't -- I don't think she disliked me. She didn't have a chance to like me or dislike me. But she just would -- she was just a woman just didn't bother, I guess, you know. I don't want to talk about her when she's
dead. She's not here to defend herself, you know.
