No, I never listened to anybody's records. I just didn't -- it wasn't that I felt that I was better than anybody else or didn't have to listen, because you can always learn something from other people, you know. It's just that I was so wrapped up in Dreamland and, you know, just going and doing my work. I didn't listen to anybody's records.
Uh-huh, now, you --
But I used to buy them for other people.
Oh, you did?
Oh, yes. And I knew she was wonderful, and I always admired her, because I thought her -- just her voice was just so outstanding, you couldn't help but admire her.
But did you ever go, for instance, if Bessie was at the Avenue, would you go to listen to her? To catch her act or anyone else's act, for that matter?
Yes, I would. Sure, because you could learn something. I could learn something from them; however, regardless of who I heard sing, I wouldn't try to sing like them. I always had my own style.
But wasn't there sort of a unity among the black performers? You know, weren't there sort of certain places where black performers used to gather, you know, some club (inaudible)?

Yes. Yes. For instance, now, every [Pekin] time after I'd leave my work at night, I'd go to the Peek-in or whatever after hour place it was, but usually I'd be working at those places. But most of the other artists would come in to listen to -- not just me, but whatever artist would be there, you know; even if I was off at night, they'd go to hear the other artists that were working at those places. We had little places that we always frequented.
And then people like Dempsey and the -- and some of the --
All the big -- all the big celebrities.
-- used to come by.

Packed all the time with the big celebrities, the people from downtown. Sometimes some of us couldn't get a place to sit because of the people from downtown because they said that we had something that they just didn't have, you know.

And then, for instance, some of the songs that we'd sing, we'd just sit there and make up something among ourselves or start humming a tune and do something like that, and no music around, and the orchestra would pick it up. Now, how

would they know what we had on our minds. It's just that -- that kindred feeling, you know. Yeah, sure, because many times I've gotten out on the floor and other people too, not just me, gotten out on the floor and start singing something, and the musicians would pick it up. Now, how would they know to go from one note to the other? But they would.
I don't know how they do it.
(Laughter)
Uh-huh. Tell me again about when you came to New York and went with Eddie Hunter's 'How Come' -- and you said all you did, you just did some numbers in the song, in the show, you didn't actually --
Just came down -- just before the finale was my spot.
And this was at the Apollo theater on 42nd Street?
That's right.
The audience there, was that a white audience?
Yes, all white.
Strictly a white audience.
Yes, oh, yes.
Uh-huh. And then you went on -- you went on the road next --
That's when the Apollo was -- oh, yes

-- that was when the Apollo was-the Apollo, was-the show of Broadway, I mean one of the theaters of Broadway, and you said the Apollo Theater on Broadway, you had made history, you know. And right today -- I don't care how big a moving picture star you are, what kind of artist you are, musically, if you haven't played Broadway, you still have missed it, you know. That's the epitome of show business, Broadway. When you play a Broadway house, then you've gone. That's the end of it.

And I was so anxious, you know, to hit that Palace. That stopped all theaters, Palace Theater. Everybody's ambition was to play the Palace. So we toured with "How Come" all over, and it was a tremendous success every place we went.
Jack Goldberg and Mr. -- it'll come to me a little later, his name --
Do you remember any of the songs you did in that show?
Yes, I did You've Got to Reap What You Sow and --
Which you wrote --
This is my -- same title but not the same words.
Oh, this isn't the one you wrote?
No, this isn't the one I wrote. This is the one that -- I forget who wrote it. I think Alexander Robinson wrote it. I used to do it in Chicago all the time.

You know? It was such a big success for me in Chicago that I -- that's what I did when I did my audition for 'How Come', 'You've Got to Reap What you Sow' and 'If You Want to Keep Your Daddy Home', I think, was the other one, and that was Porter Grainger.
Now, the last time we did -- we covered more or less the '20's, but we didn't mention -- you got married. When did you get married?

Yeah. I went to -- from Dreamland I had a contract for good money to go to Cincinnati, Ohio. So -- a place called Michaelson's in Cincinnati. I went to Cincinnati and opened in Michaelson's, oh, looked like the Lord had his arms around me, Chris. It was such a big success, I -- and this fellow, Willard Saxbe Townsend was his name. He was a very handsome man and a waiter.

And I married him. That was -- put it down. I have it someplace.
We'll get back to that.

Yes, anyhow I married Willard, and he came back to Chicago, back to the Dreamland. Well, Willard was such a nice fellow -- he was a perfect gentleman, a fine fellow -- he came back to Chicago with me. Lord, it's a shame the way I treated him. Came back to Chicago and he wanted -- the fellows around Chicago, you know, the ones that were in the sporting life, they wanted him to just hang around, you
know, and see me work, and I had never had that on my mind, you know.

So I told him to get a job, you know. And so because I worked late -- I was working at Dreamland and an after hour place too -- why, he didn't want to get up in the morning to go and look for work and -- because I was sleeping. So I told him to just try to find another place to go.
(Laughter)

So anyhow he -- I made up my mind that I didn't want to be bothered. So I think that's the first time I went to Europe. I either went to Europe or went to New York. Anyhow I left him, and he got married.
So when I opened in Showboat -- I must tell you this -- when I was in Showboat --
In London in 1929.

-- in London, yes -- I received a letter from him saying he just didn't -- a note to the woman who had won. He didn't want to prove on my success and all, but just a note to the woman who had won, because he had gone to school in Canada and got a degree in commercial --
Art?

-- art -- no, no, not commercial art, commercial -- business, you know, because he became the president of the Redcaps here in New York. See? He said, just a note, because, you know, to the woman who had won

because of my success in making him a success, because had I let him hang around, you know, and not do any work and just hang around there and accept the nickels and dimes from the people where I'm singing, you know, he would have never made a man of himself. So I made a man of him.
I see.

See? And he became -- oh, he was quite a big man, because when I -- this is, you know, after, but when I was in Tokyo, I was going to Yokahama, and we crossed on the ocean. He was going to attend to some business for the commercial -- the Redcaps -- they didn't call them Redcaps, but anyhow --
Porters --
Well, they didn't call them porters. Anyhow, the redcaps -- it was the redcaps.
Oh, the redcaps.
Yes, he was the president of it. He was going to do business over in -- there for the union because he was the only Negro on the executive board of the CIO. So I helped him a lot, didn't I?
Yes.

Yeah. And we were the best of friends. We were the -- when I came back from Europe and all, we used to go out to dinner and all and just good platonic friends. But we used to talk of my success and his, and he finally died.

He died, uh-huh. But he was a wonderful young man. He was a fine young man. And his father -- his grandfather, poor old man, used to come while I was in Cincinnati with a little basket on his arms bringing me vegetables out of the garden. Wasn't that lovely?
(Laughter)
So what -- now, let's talk about London in 1929. How did you get that job with Showboat?
With Showboat?
Yes.

Well, I tell you, I went from -- I went from New York to Monte Carlo just on a visit, took a friend of mine, a girlfriend of mine, Bert Williams' oldest niece, Lottie Tyler. So we went to Monte Carlo just -- a little fun. And while I was there --
That's quite a trip to go for just a little -- you must have been making very good money.

I was doing all right, yeah, making a lot of money. I went to Monte Carlo, and while I was there -- I had -- when I got there -- I had been trying from New York to get entrance to England, but you couldn't get in without a labor permit before entering England.
So while I was in Monte Carlo, I received a letter, a telegram from Noble Sissle of Sissle and Blake, and it said, if you want to come in to London, to England, come on your own,

pay your own transportation and all your own expenses, and just mention the Lord Mayor's name at the border if you will do a benefit performance for the flood sufferers -- they had had a flood there -- for the flood sufferers.

Immediately I jumped to that. So I went from Monte Carlo to London to do this benefit, and while doing the benefit Sir Alfred Butt, Oscar Hammerstein and Jerome Kern were in the audience, and they heard me. And a fellow named Leslie Hutchinson, who Bobby Short sounds exactly alike, played for me, never had a rehearsal or anything, played for me.
Is he the one who used to write for the Chicago Defender, isn't it?
No, Leslie Hutchinson was --
Oh, that's Huggins.

Yeah, Leslie Hutchinson was the biggest thing in England at the time. He put his handkerchief in his sleeve, a pianist, and sang his own songs. Oh, he was the last word. So he played for me. And Mr. Butt and him happened to be in the audience they heard me. But they didn't say anything to me then; however, I was stopping at 17 Regents Park Road. That's where Marian Anderson and I lived, 17 Regents Park Road. And I received a call to come down to Drury Lane Theater to sing -- to do an audition for Showboat.
I went. But in the meantime there was a woman, a

white woman named Maizie Ailing who was absolutely marvelous. She was the last word. She was a big woman, just what they wanted in Aunt Jemimy, and had the voice and -- she just had everything that you want. And she -- she sang, and then I sang.
You were vying for the same part?

Same part, Queenie, in Showboat with Paul Robeson. So I sang -- she sang first, and she was marvelous. And I had no sense about worrying, you know. I just went on out there and sang, because I always tried to be natural, you know, and I sang. So then I get a note saying -- no, I looked in -- yes, I get a note saying I had the part. And the newspaper came out and said why they chose me was because Mr. Hammerstein and Sir Alfred Butt and Jerome Kern said they wanted the real thing. Maizie Ailing was wonderful, but they wanted the real thing, and they had found it in me. So that's how I got the job.
Do you remember what you sang?

Yes. Just let me see -- I sang 'Just Another Day Wasting Away' -- 'Just Another Day Wasting Away' -- da-da-da-da-dum. I've forgotten now, but anyhow 'Just Another Day Wasting Away', and what else was the other song? I believe I sang 'If You Want To Keep Your Daddy Home.' That song was always a success for me. Yeah. Let me see --
Had you heard --
If you can't keep your daddy home, don't cry -- if you can't keep your good man home, don't cry when he's gone. That's what I sang.
Now, had you heard Showboat before any?
No, uh-uh.
Could you -- now, as a black person, could you go into a Broadway theater, for instance, the original Showboat. You could have gone --
Uh-huh.
-- you were not barred from that. I mean you could --
You mean where, in America?
Yes, in a Broadway show, you know, a -- in a white theater downtown back in the '20's.
Well, I think I'd have to -- well, I did have to dress in Aunt Jemimy clothes, but I would have to have dressed in Aunt Jemimy clothes, yes.
To be in the audience?
Yeah. What do you mean? I don't quite --
Well, you know, Showboat opened on Broadway, right? And could you, if you had been here then, and I guess you were here, could you go in, could you buy a ticket to Showboat and go in?
Well, at that particular --
Were you allowed in the theater? I mean were black people allowed --
In the '20's?
Yes.
Well, I think they more or less -- they were more or less segregated, if they let them in at all. You'd have to sit up in the gallery and not the mezzanine.
Oh, I see.
The gallery --
Now, that reminds me --

Now, in -- in places like Baltimore and Washington and those places you couldn't sit in -- they wouldn't let you in some of the theaters at all; however, 'Mamba's Daughters' was the first black company to play the National Theater in Washington and the first black company to play the Empire at 40th and Broadway. That was history because that was the theater for that kind of -- for dramatic things, you know.
Yes. But when you said in the balcony, it reminded me of Nigger Heaven. They used to call that Nigger Heaven.
Uh-huh.
Do you remember when that book came out?
Carl van Vechten
Yes, very well, Carlton Beck, yes
There was a lot of scandal -- protests about it. People protested it. But they finally found what he meant.
Well, I understand that a lot of people who protested it never actually read the book.
That's exactly right.
It was the title --

That's what happens today. A lot of things today happen where people say different things, and they misinterpret those things. Now, I'm a Negro girl, but I don't have any qualms about this and the other. I use my own judgment. That's the reason people never get me in any of this wild stuff that they're pulling sometime.

I use my own judgment. Nobody leads me, because I want to tell you something. When I was in Paris -- I'll never forget this -- in Paris. Was that Paris or London? Anyhow, a fellow came and interview -- was talking to me, and he was trying to get me -- the way he was trying to worm around, he was trying to get me to say things about America, and I was too slick for him, you see.
And if I know anything, if I remember correctly, it was the -- what they call -- a Worker?
The paper -- the -- oh, yeah, the communist paper?
Yes. It was the Worker.
Daily Worker.

Daily Worker, and he even had put my picture in there and everything in this Daily Worker, but he couldn't say that I said anything against my government because I didn't. I am an American all the way. You understand? And I was too slick for him.
Well, that's like when they made up the story about Bessie having been turned away from a white hospital. It never happened.

Yes, I mean that's awful. See, I don't believe those things, and a lot of us, a lot of colored people will read things and misinterpret them. They get the wrong meaning. You understand? That's right. So this guy, he thought he was being smart. I didn't realize that he was really getting me to talk against my country until something he said, but he said in a way, had I not been alert, he would have gotten me to say the wrong thing.

But I was alert and I realized what he was doing, after having talked with him for some time, you see. He wanted to know, well, how do they treat you? I said, they treat me fine. I said, I -- my God, I'm making a living. I'm living. I said, and anybody that has ambition and wants to make it, they can make it. They don't stop you from trying to make it.
And I said, if you can't make it in America, you can't make it anyplace. I was telling him everything, child.
And when I realized, I guess he said, well, we don't want to talk to her anymore because she's the wrong kind.

Now, I remember reading in the Chicago Defender from -- I believe it was 1931 -- very early '30's anyway -- there was a long article about some problems Duke Ellington was having and had had in London, getting a hotel room, and I recall when they found out that he wasn't West Indian, everything was okay.
Uh-huh, yes.
But when they thought he was West Indian, then --
Because, you know, during the war they told the West Indians -- the West Indians wanted to go back and help. They said, no, don't come. Stay where you are. They didn't want them.
I think that was around the time you were in London, 1929. And now you were performing at the Drury Lane with people like Sir Cedric Hardwicke and --
Uh-huh, and Mary Burks --
-- (unintelligible) --

-- Sir Cedric Hardwicke. No, yeah, Fay Compton -- not Fay Compton -- oh, what was Parthy's name? She played the part of Parthy, played the part of Parthy. Compton was her last name, though. Oh, it'll come to me. Yes, uh-huh.
Now --

I tell you who got Paul mixed up in that -- that communism and stuff. Paul wasn't mixed up in that. That -- the woman, Lady Astor, used to come back there and talk to him all the time. Several of those people would come and talk to Paul, and he was just a nice fellow, you know. Paul was very -- even though he was a big man, big athlete, he was soft.

But his wife, Essie, who always wanted to be white, used to talk Paul into a lot of that stuff. That's right. Paul didn't -- he didn't go in for that communism. Paul thought he was just -- what he was just saying was just to help his race. He didn't mean to be against his government. You understand?
Yeah, of course.
He didn't mean to be against his government. Paul only meant to be a good fellow, and if he can help poor people that are not as fortunate as he is, he wanted to help them.
Then his government turned against him.

That's right, unfortunately, they turned against him, but Paul did not mean to go against his government. I was right there at Drury Lane working opposite Paul, right there every night in the theater with him, and I
know that he did not mean to be -- to be a communist.
Was there any -- problem -- now, you worked with white performers every night, and did you -- did you socialize with them, and wasn't -- when the curtain went down, you didn't just --
Well, I never socialized with white nor black. I'm not --
You're antisocial?

I'm not antisocial. But I like to be alone. See? Oh, we were -- at the theater we were friendly and hello this, and we didn't visit -- I didn't visit them, and I never asked them to visit me. You see? And they didn't ask me to visit them. But they would have, and I suppose, had I been a little more sociable, I would have asked them.

But I -- when I finished my work, I always wanted to go home and go to bed, not that I slept a lot, but I used to like to read a lot. I read a lot, you know. I wanted to keep up with the events of the day, you know, and everything that was going on, and I read a lot.

So I hate to hear people sit up and talk and don't know anything to talk about, you know. And you know another thing? Now, I just said it, which is a terrible thing. Every time you hear people being interviewed, the first thing they say -- you know -- you know -- you know -- why don't they try not to say you know so much. It's very, very annoying to
the listener.
If you know, you don't have to be told.
That's right. The listener -- we don't like to hear it every minute. You know so and so -- you know so and so -- everything is so and so and so, you know. Why don't they stop that?
It's like some people say uh-uh --
Don't they?
It's a habit. It's a habit.
It's a habit.
I was going to ask you now -- during that time --
We'll go back to a whole lot of things, won't we?
Oh, sure.
Oh, good.
Anytime you feel that you think of (unintelligible) something, by all means (inaudible).
Okay.
But during that time in Europe it was quite different from being here. I mean it had to be, you know, for a black performer in Europe, it had to be -- there had to be a difference.
Well, I tell you what --
Attitudes, right?

I want to tell you, Chris -- excuse me for cutting you off, but the thing of it was, when you were a celebrity, when you went to Europe, even the most prejudiced parts, you were put on a pedestal. The people in Europe would put you on a pedestal whereby even from you leave America, you'd have to go to Europe in order to make a name -- you would make a name quicker, I'd say, in Europe, and then when you came back to America, you were recognized.
Yeah, sometimes it's still that way.

Well, I'm telling you, they -- you go to Europe -- when I -- now, when -- my goodness, when I came back from Europe after having played 'Showboat,' why my -- I was on a pedestal. I got contracts from every way, you know. So I dare say -- you know, there again --
(Laughter)
But how long did 'Showboat' run?
'Showboat' ran about 11 1/2 months. Now, I tell you, there was a little jealousy there in 'Showboat'. Edith Day, who was our star -- when the --
That's who I was thinking of.
-- when the notices came out the next day about the show, having spoken so beautiful of Paul, saying that Paul was this and the other and he was -- Viola Compton -- don't forget --
Viola --

-- that Paul was so tremendous in his voice, which was like a bell -- like a bell tolling in the distance. He was a marvelous man; his voice was just something -- said that he was so wonderful and this and the other. Edith Day became jealous, although she was a very fine actress and was American -- she was American. But she had lived in Europe so long, you see.

But that little jealous feeling was there, and that was what broke up the show. However, we traveled -- and that particular show did not travel. They did have a number two show that traveled, but not with us. We didn't travel. We stayed at Drury Lane the time we were there. See?
And then I got a --
Did the King attend the performance?

In London? Oh, yes. The King and Queen -- the old mother King and Queen. Now, listen -- Paul, bless his heart -- I love him so -- but you know what happened? They came, and they -- I don't know whether they should have told us, but they did tell us. And Paul came out tto sing Old Man River and went off pitch and stayed off.
He was nervous.
Nervous -- singing Old Man River -- nervous. And I think it was bad for them to tell him, because when I was in the theater, I didn't want anybody to tell me

when they were coming. Don't tell me you're coming. Just be there, and then after the show, tell me. I never tell a performer, I'll see you tonight; I'll be at the theater. After the theater, if they have time to accept me or let me come back, all right. But otherwise, okay just the same. But I never would tell a performer that.
And that's what hurt Paul.
Now, after "Showboat" -- it's strange you didn't make any -- did you make any records in London at that time?
In London what did I -- Yes. When did I make --
Let's see.
-- didn't I make "Two Cigarettes in the Dark" with Jack -- well, not records. Yes, I did. I made --
Did you do that song, "Two Cigarettes in the Dark?"
I introduced it for Noel Coward.
Really?
That and "Miss Otis Regrets." So don't let Vic Top tell you she introduced it. I introduced it.
Well, how did that come about?
Well, Vic sings it all the time. How did that come about? Well, Mr. Coward used to frequent the Dorchester all the time, you know, and the King -- he was the

Prince of Wales at that time. And they used to come in, and I used to sing different songs, and I guess he just thought my voice was all right and asked me to do 'Two Cigarettes in the Dark,' which I did. And what else did I do? Oh, 'Miss Otis Regrets'. I did 'Miss Otis', and 'I Travel Alone' -- very smart song. You -- this is one of the smartest songs you ever heard.

He asked me to do it, and I made a test record for him of 'I Travel Alone'. I used to sing it down to the Bon Soir when I was here, but it was a -- it's a smart song. I've never heard anybody do it -- very smart. That was his. So that's how I happened to do those songs. I introduced them.
That 'Two Cigarettes in the Dark,' that's a beautiful thing. That's what I told him --
I heard it the other day.
Did you hear it? Where did you hear it?
I have a recording of it by some -- a man singing it.

Well, I tell you, that's what they just sent me the other day, honey. That's what they just sent me the other day, sent me five records -- and me singing 'Two Cigarettes in the Dark' with Jack Jackson's Band in London at the Dorchester. One of the fellows -- did I -- no, I'll bring it over next time -- sent me --
Yes, that's --
-- he wrote me a letter saying that he had just met Elizabeth Welsh, who -- a good friend of his, and she spoke about me, and he asked her to give him my address. And incidentally, his name is Chris.
(Laughter)

And she gave him my address, and he wrote me and said that he had some records. I think he has a record company there and that he thought that I would enjoy listening to them. So he sent me -- he sent me one at first, and then he sent me five more. So I'll bring one over to you. Yes, I think you'd like it.
Now, then you -- did you after that closed, after Showboat closed, did you then go back to the States before going to Paris, or did you go straight to Paris?

I went back to -- oh, no. When Showboat closed, I toured all -- toured the theaters in th e provinces of England. The Argyle Theater -- oh, I hope I can find that record -- I mean that article, just a beautiful article. I think I was the first colored girl ever worked there.

I made the way for a lot of things, you know, in England. Yes. And they were so wonderful to me. I sang at that theater, and then I got contracts -- all the provinces -- Liverpool and Scotland and Ireland. And let me see -- I played the Palace in Dublin, and I played the Limerick --
Savoy in Limerick, and I played the Palace in -- I played all over. I've got the contracts. I'll show you -- all over the provinces of England.
And then I introduced 'Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day.' That was a beautiful success for me.
Oh, where did you introduce that?
In -- 'Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day,' at the -- oh, that was in Liverpool. I introduced that song, 'Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day.' And speaking about -- oh, I want to come to that next.
Well, speaking of introducing something, how about 'Some Day, Sweetheart?'
'Some Day' -- but I introduced that in Chicago. I introduced that --
Chicago, y es. A lot of people I've talked to, older people from that period, remember you as the lady who introduced 'Some Day, Sweetheart.'

Yes, I certainly did, some -- and I introduced 'A Good Man's Hard to Find.' And I introduced -- what's that thing that -- oh, let me come back to it. It'll -- uh-huh -- anyhow, let me see now. There's another song I introduced. Oh, I introduced 'St. Louis Blues', you know.
No, I didn't know that.
In England, yes. Yeah. And I introduced the Black Bottom Dance in England. I'll bring you that
article. I've got them all here someplace.
Now, there is this picture of you and -- from a show in Paris --
Casino de Paris?
-- with a huge cage behind you --
Casino de Paris.
-- and a white chorus line dressed like birds -- dressed like birds --
That's right.
-- sitting perched up on a pole like birds --

That's right, Casino de Paris. Well, I tell you what, when Josephine Baker went to the Folies-Bergere, that's when Mr. Barner, who had the Casino de Paris, had me come down, and I don't think I did an audition for -- for the Casino de Paris. I didn't do an audition for Casino de Paris because he had -- had heard me at the Grande Ecart in Paris, a smart little nightclub, and I was dressed by Jean Patou.
(Tape Four)
And he had seen me in -- at the Grand Ecart, and he just had me come down and go to work in the Casino de Paris.
So did you -- no, you didn't have any management firm or manager -- all these bookings in
No.
-- you handled that all yourself?

Yes. Now, I tell you what -- Gustav Wally, when I was in the Casino de Paris, I went in after Josephine -- Gustav Wally, who was the grandson of the King of Sweden, was in the show with me, called -- and Cecile Sorel, who was the woman, the Sarah Bernhardt of France -- she -- it was Vive Paris, the name of the show -- she was the star of the show.

And Gustav Wall was in this show, who was the grandson of the King of Sweden, and I was -- we were talking. I -- he was a dancer, but a lousy one, but he was very good. He was the sweetest thing in the world, Chris. And he would -- we'd get to talking. So he said to me -- I said -- he told me he was from the Scandinavian countries, you know, from up that way.

So I said, oh, I'd love to go. And I said -- he said, I tell you what. If you ever want to go to Denmark, you write -- write Bach -- her name was Bach, Mrs. Bach. Her first name will come to me. She was the artistic director of this -- of the National Scholar in Copenhagen. He said, if you ever want to go, you just tell her that I told you to come.
Now, listen -- I told you to come, and just mention
my name, and you will get a contract. Do you know that woman had never seen me or anything. She sent me a contract for six months just from his word. I opened there at the National Scholar.
This was in the '30's.

Yes, in the '30's. I'll bring some of the programs to you so you can see them. I think it's '34, '35, '36. I had standing contracts after that to go twice a year. I opened at the National Scholar with the Edgar Well Thomas' Band. Edgar Well Thomas, he had a band, and he was tremendous.

I worked with him, and thank the Lord, I was a tremendous success. I'd leave out of the Scholar, which was the big theater, and go right downstairs in the little bar, the little bar downstairs. And the fellow that played there, I hope I can think of his name, Chris. He was marvelous.

And I worked with him, and then certain nights of the week I'd go out to the old Lorry. Miss Bach's father was out there, and he liked me so well, I sang Kentucky Home, and they put it in the chimes. Isn't that wonderful? And whenever he was there, I'd sing that, and then he'd go home -- go and go to bed. Wasn't that wonderful?
Yes.
So from then on I would go to Copenhagen, back to Copenhagen, back again, back to Copenhagen,
just month after month.
His name wasn't Leo, the pianist, Matisse?
No. I think I have it written down in one of the programs. I'll bring it to you.
Uh-huh. Now, when you -- so you spent a great deal of time in Europe in the '30's then?
Uh-huh.
Were you going back and forth --
Back and forth --
-- to the States?
Yes.
Coming back to the States --
Yes, I came back to the States. I think I stayed three or four years one time.

Because, well, you had to have been back, because I know in 1935 you were recording those things we talked about before with Fats Waller, the unissued things in New York. Then in 1939 you were with Decca.
But now, listen here, now, '35, if you remember now -- when did I go to the Palladium, because I remember in 1935, that's when I made that picture.
Oh, yes, tell me about that. Now --
So I --
-- this was the first color movie
made in England.

In England -- now, that was -- Reginald Forsyte wrote the song -- Dark Shadows. And this was a big picture, and my sequence was the last sequence in th e -- in the picture, but it was a big choir behind me, and we had on those big gowns like the choir singers, you know, sing and all.
Oh, the robes?
The robes and things, yes, and we sang this song. And the -- had a beautiful write-up about it, beautiful write-up.
This was a -- this was a system, a color system --
Color -- the first time they had ever used it.
It wasn't technicolor. It was another system from (inaudible).
Another system altogether. The first time they'd ever used this color system. And I think I have the little -- little things that go in -- like you run it. I think I've got some of them.
Oh, really -- I'd like to see those.
Yes, now, incidentally, talk --
The name of the film was what?
Radio Parade of '35. Radio Parade of

1935. That was it, Radio Parade of 1935. And the Casino de Paris, as I say, was Vive Paris with Cecile Sorel. Don't forget her because she was a marvelous woman, the actress of France, you know. And incidentally, talking about Showboat, don't forget now, Mabel Mercer was in the choir, in the big choir that sang. I'll bring you the picture and show you.
Oh, she's always -- now, you talk about a lady. They don't -- oh, what a lady.
Do you still see her?
Do I? We're the best of friends. Sure, Jimmy and Mabel and Brick and all of us, we get together. That's my group. We get together and --
Jimmy Daniels.

Yes, Jimmy Daniels. We fix big dinners and things and we -- just us -- we get to talking about Paris. And incidentally, one of the places in Paris where Brick has one of her nightclubs, I'm sitting -- Mabel, Brick -- no, Brick is standing. A little fellow named Louie Coles, who was -- oh, he was marvelous. Everybody was crazy about him. He was a marvelous little singer and dancer.
Now, Jimmy Donahue, you know, Jimmy -- you know Jimmy Donahue of the Woolworth millions? Well, he was the one that sang Long Live Haile Selassie during the war when he was in Italy.
(Laughter)
Jimmy was a mess. He's Barbara Hutton's cousin. Yeah, he yelled out, Long Live Haile Selassie. Lord have mercy, and they put him -- I think they put him in jail. I don't know.
(Laughter)
Well, we all have pictures at Brick's, you know. That's what we used to do at night, you know. We'd all go to some other club or go to Brick's club, you know, in Paris.
Now, you must have met Josephine Baker when you were in Paris in the '30's.

Met her in Paris? I met Josephine before she ever went to Paris. I tell you how she happened to go to Paris. Josephine, when they had Shuffle Along -- Sissle and Blake had Shuffle Along. They had a little girl that stood on the end of the chorus line -- Josephine was on the end of the chorus line and used to clown and carry on, on the end of the chorus line before she heard of Paris, when she was a little kid like.

Josephine was only about 15 or 16 years old when she first went to Paris, you know, not a day older, very -- now, who was a wonderful singer, they sent for Maude de Forrest and several people, they sent to come to Paris. When they got to Paris, Maude de Forrest, as some people do, lost her head. She thought they couldn't do without her.
And Josephine stepped -- they put Josephine right in

her place, and that was the making of Josephine Baker. That was -- they -- she had a beautiful body, as she still had when she died. She would -- Maude de Forrest, they just gave Maude her walking papers and put the bananas on Josephine with her -- that yellow bananas and her beautiful brown body, and she just tore the show up. So that was the making of Josephine Baker. That was the beginning of Josephine Baker.
Just like when -- when -- I ain't going say it because I like Gertrude --
Well, Gertrude, I've always felt, made the mistake of her life --
That's what I was going to tell you.
-- when she left Shuffle Along.
Exactly. When she felt that they couldn't do without her when she left Shuffle Along, Florence Mills stepped in, and that was the beginning of Florence Mills.
And the end of Gertrude Saunders.
And the end of Gertrude Saunders. She never did anything after that, never.
Somebody must have lured her away thinking that --
That she couldn't be done without. That's right. It's bad, you know. You can be done without.
Did you ever meet Florence Mills? You must have.
Honey, I knew Florence. Florence and I were good friends.
(Inaudible).

Like a little bird, she was the daintiest little thing and the sweetest little lady you ever saw in your life and had a voice. She never could record. Isn't that funny? Her voice never -- never took. They tried to make it, but she couldn't -- her voice would never --
Too tiny.

Too tiny, but like a musical -- it was just -- big as Paul's was musical, hers was little and musical, the sweetest little voice you ever heard. That's what she was like and a little lady at all times. And you know who I want you to meet?
How could she be heard?
Huh?
How would she be heard from the stage?

I don't know. But when she'd walk out on the stage, and we didn't have microphones at that time, you know, when she'd walk out on the stage, you could hear a pin fall, and she could -- oh, when she sang 'I'm a Little Blackbird Looking For a Bluebird,' she was -- you -- everybody just loved her. She was just so dainty and sweet. Now, I'd like for you to meet her husband, Chris.
He's still around?

Yes. No kidding. I'll call him sometime. Now, they had the Labor Day Parade. I'm going to tell you how Florence was coming back -- we -- the Labor Day Parade, for instance, like today in Paris, and Florence, little kid and I, we got on the top of a car and went to this parade.
And Florence left the next morning for America, and she never came back. She died.
She died on the way back to --
No, she got back to America and had -- what do you call it, tonsillitis, I believe it was.
Yeah, she was young.

Yes, oh, very young. She had a sister named Maude -- Maude Mills. Maude tried to make it, but she could never make it. She was a little -- little heavier than -- I mean -- I don't mean physically, but she wasn't dainty like Florence.
Now, Gertrude Saunders, I always felt, listening to Gertrude Saunders, that if -- if she hadn't been black, she might have become an opera singer.
Her voice --
Yes.
Yes.
It was -- had that operatic quality.
That's right. And so many people tried to imitate her, you know. They tried to imitate Gertrude, but they could never do what she did.
Uh-huh. Now, speaking of opera singers, did you ever hear Sissqretta Jones?
No, I tell you who -- she was called Black Patty.
Black Patty, right.
Uh-huh, Black Patty. Well, she was a friend of Mrs. Williams and them, but I never met her. Bert Williams and --
You knew of her?
Yes. Oh, everybody knew of her. If you didn't see her, you read about her, didn't you? Yes. Oh, yes, Sissqretta Jones. And Ada Walker, Ada Overton Walker --
Sure --

With George Walker and Williams and Walker -- no, I never saw them and never met them, but I -- I never saw George Walker and Ada Walker, but I knew Bert Williams and Mrs. Williams because she came to the ship with me when I sailed for Europe the first time, Bert Williams' wife with his nieces because, as I say, she went with me, his oldest niece, Lottie.
Uh-huh. I saw a thing in the Chicago Defender, an article. There was a picture of Mae West.
There was a picture of Ada Overton Walker. And it said, Ada Overton Walker was the real queen of Paris.

She was, she really was. She was. They say she -- I never saw her, but they tell me she was a knockout because Miss Williams had pictures all over, naturally, of course. It was Williams and Walker, you know. And let me see. What did I have I wanted to show you? Something I wanted to show you. I brought this letter from the Courier, where the --
Do you -- did that film you did ever show here in this country, the -- that --
I don't know.
-- English film?
I think it did, because I think somebody told me. If I'm not mistaken, I think somebody told me they saw that film. But I didn't see it. But I understand that it was very good, very good.
Did you ever meet Isadora Duncan?
No.
You didn't?
No. I read a lot about him. He's the one that went barefoot, isn't he?
She --
She, I mean.
She was a dancer.
Yes. No, I never met her, eccentric lady.
Very eccentric.
Uh-huh. No, I never met her.
Because she was in Europe (in-audible).
And let's see. Something else I wanted to tell you, Chris. You've got that stuff about me playing George M.Cohan Theater, didn't you, and the part -- we're coming back -- we come back?
No. Yeah, you can talk about that now.
All right. Well now, you see, when "How Come" -- after "How Come" there was another show called "Struttin' Time".
Oh, what was that?
That was -- we played the George M. Cohan Theater, and we went -- that -- now, George M. Cohan Theater was a real theater too, real Broadway theater.
It was?
Yes, down where the Hippodrome was, you know. You didn't know the Hippodrome. That's before your time.
No, I know of the Hippodrome. That's a huge place.
Yes, uh-huh. Well, that was --
(Inaudible) Where you brought the family.

Yes, that's right. That's right. Well, that's where the -- the Hippodrome is where this girl, Catherine Yarborough, the first Negro opera singer, you know, that -- in later years she changed her name to Katrina Jarbora because she lost her head and missed out. She's around now. I see her all the time.

But what was I telling you? Oh, about "Struttin' Time." We played, and Mr. Grisman, Sam Grisman, Sam Grisman -- this show was -- oh, was a tremendous success. I don't know what happened that the show closed, but we -- but we -- after the George M. Cohan we toured, you know, went around the different theaters.
Now, who wrote "Struttin' Time?"
Lucky Roberts and -- was it Lucky Roberts and them? Elrich Rogers and Lucky Roberts. They were wonderful singers. He wrote --
Lucky used to accompany Bert Williams.
Lucky Roberts?
Piano.
I don't know that. Did he? Well, Lucky Roberts wrote a beautiful song here a few years ago, you know, da-da-da-da-da-dah, da-da, da-da, he wrote that.
He wrote --
He used to own a little club in Harlem.

That's right. He wrote some beautiful music. Now, his -- he and Elich Rogers -- Lucky always wrote the music, and Elich Rogers wrote the words. And the music was beautiful -- beautiful music. And now, that's when -- that was the early years when colored song -- colored writers were out of this world, you know? Well, he and Lucky and Elich Rogers wrote some beautiful tunes.
Now, what else did I want to --
Struttin' Time, do you remember any of the songs from that? Was that like How Come? I mean did you just come out and do some songs and he played for you?
No, I was all the way through. I had a big part in that.
You did. What was that about?
I've forgotten. I'll ask somebody.
(Laughter)
I'll ask somebody. Harry'll tell me. My brother, he'll tell me. I think he was in it. And he was in How Come too.
Oh, he was?
Yeah. He'll tell me all about Struttin' Time, because I'll ask him about Struttin' Time, but anyhow, there was some gorgeous music.
He's not really your brother.
No.
We don't want to confuse people.

No, no. I don't have no -- no, I just call him my brother. 'Magnolia' -- a song called 'Magnolia', 'Magnolia, You Could if You Would. Magnolia, magnolia, I wish that you could -- wish that you would.' It's a beautiful song, some beautiful music in struttin' time. And let me see what else.

Who else was in that show? Oh, this girl I was telling you about, Katrina Jarbora, she was in it. Catherine Yarborough was her name, who lost her head. She's right here. I like Catherine. She's a nice kid. But funny how we lose our heads so quick. Isn't it funny? Can't stand success, prosperity.
If you get -- you know, you can get to the top of the hill and stumble and fall, can't you?
Sure.
Why do people get excited?
Still happens.

It happens, doesn't it? Now, here's another thing I want to ask you, Chris. This has nothing to do with what you're doing, but I want to ask you. Why is it that the performers of today -- you know, we were taught that, if you're an artist, you don't get out on the street and sell

your wares right out on the corner and all that. We wouldn't do that. You couldn't -- you couldn't pay an old time performer to start singing his songs on the bus or on the corner and all that. We wouldn't do that. Where's the refinement?
It's gone.

It has, because we -- you know what, when we walked out on the stage? They would criticize your bows, how you would enter and exit. You had to exit properly. You had to enter properly and exit properly. You didn't come out on the stage, and after you got there, wouldn't know what to do?
So that's like --

And you didn't have to have no training for it. You understand? Some people did, but some didn't. And most of us didn't. We didn't have money to pay for training. So we'd walk out and be natural. But some -- people are being so unnatural. And why is it -- oh, Lord, I don't want to get away from this thing, but why do they start, why don't they try to speak distinctly, and when they sing a song, why not let us understand the words?
That was very important, wasn't it?
Most important. When you walked out on the stage, if you weren't correct, if your entrance, your exit, if you didn't speak correctly -- you understand? If people

couldn't -- they'd get in the back of the house, the people would, you know. For instance, some person that had paid for a ticket would go to the management and said, I didn't understand what she was saying. You understand?
Demand their money back.
Absolutely. But today you don't -- it's supposed to -- some of our biggest stars, you don't know a thing they're saying.
That's right.
A couple of girls, I don't want to call their names now because I enjoy the music and their voices, but I wish they would speak plain enough for me to understand what they're saying.
That's why on a lot of records nowadays they print the lyrics, and it's the only way --
Well, they should -- they should, because I would -- oh, I just enjoyed some of the girls. I would enjoy them so much if I could understand what they're saying.
You do enjoy music, what you hear today?
You do. You do. I mean that's not -- that's why people enjoying the old songs and the old artists, they're coming back. They're coming back.
That's right.

They are coming back. Look at Bing Crosby. You walk out there, you listen to Perry Como, you listen to Bing Crosby, you listen to the different old artists, and what a pleasure-- what a pleasure. Now, that will take me back to theaters. I stopped going for a while. But I'll go back to the theater if I --
To hear --

-- to listen to the older people. That's right. And Bobby Short, he's a younger type, a later type, but you understand every word he says. And Mabel Mercer, of course, she has no comparison. She's just in a class by herself.
Now, there's a lady who pronounces every word.
Every word.
When was the last time you sang?
The last time I sang? When I made my records in '61.
For me?
Yeah.
Oh, really? You haven't sung since then. And you hadn't -- were you singing up to that point?
No.
You had stopped?
Yeah, I had stopped.
You had such a powerful voice in '61 when you recorded for me.
(Laughter)
And I hadn't sung a word before the --
You were so tiny and this big voice coming out.
And the day before -- the day before I recorded I hadn't opened my mouth, because I never sing around the house or anything, you know, never, uh-uh.
Boy, you'd never know it.
But you know when -- if I would just, for instance, sing a couple of songs a day for two or three days, I could bait out again, you know. Yeah, because I don't abuse my voice. I don't drink or smoke.
That's right.
See? And I certainly don't carouse. I do not -- I don't keep late hours. When I do my work, I go home.
Did you ever drink or smoke?
Never in my life. And, for instance, to smell liquor makes me kind of ill. Uh-huh. I don't even like to smell it.
I don't drink, but I smoke.
Yeah, well, but you're so nice otherwise, Chris. I don't mean to embarrass you, but I mean you're
such a gentleman otherwise. A little smoking ain't going hurt you. But I never did drink or smoke. No. That's the reason some of the girls used to say I was a dicty entertainer, dicty meant --
I know. It's like the black waiters in the White House.
That's right. That's right, exactly. Yeah.
Now, what about -- but you did go to some after hours places, like the Pekin...
Oh, yeah, well, I worked in them, so I had to go in them.
That's right (inaudible).
Most of the time I was working in them. So I had to be there. But after that I'd go on home. See?
Yeah, which was unusual for someone who was in show business.

That's right. And that's the reason, while I was in France, the Frenchmen could never understand the fact, when they'd ask me to have a drink, I'd always drink lemonade or something, you know. They -- 'Vous ne buvez pas?' you know? Don't smoke, don't drink? No, I don't drink or smoke.
Now, when you were in France or in Copenhagen or London or wherever, were there moments where you
really longed to go back to Harlem or just --
You mean work in Harlem?
Well, work or just sort of get the atmosphere of Harlem or Chicago or go home, were you homesick?

Well, I don't say that I was homesick, but there were times when I would want to go back. Now, for instance, every time I would leave Chicago and come to New York to record, I couldn't get back to Chicago fast enough. I always left on the next train.

Now, when I was in Europe, when I -- now, I remember when I was singing at Fred Payne's Artist Club in Paris. I -- there was a song-- when the -- what is that -- there was -- "some in clover the white cliffs of Dover"--
It's called The White Cliffs of Dover.
Yeah, oh, that song made me homesick several times. I used to stand up there at the piano and cry like a baby. You know, that's when, I think, the war was going on, wasn't it?
Yes, that was -- that was a big song then.
Yes. Oh, what a song. And I -- then I did go back to America. I got homesick.
Now, you did go back in 1936 to America, and you went to Connie's Inn. I think we briefly --
Did I --
-- mentioned that you were at Connie's Inn. Now, at that time that would have to be Connie's Inn down on Broadway.
Yeah.
Right?
That's the four corners of Broadway, 48th, 49th -- let me see. 47th and 48th and 7th and 40 --
Which later became the Latin Quarter.
That's right, the Four Corners.
And now it's a porno movie house.
That's right. Oh, it is? My Lord.
Cine Lido has been there -- but it's still the same building. And I was just wondering what -- what was that like? What was Connie then like?
Connie's Inn was wonderful. Louie Armstrong was playing there, you know.
Sure.
And Louis Russell's Band. And it was packed all the time. They had beautiful girls.
Did they have tables?
Yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes, it was a beautiful place.
And what was the dressing rooms like
Is that so?
-- little closets, you know.

Well, we had nice dressing rooms, because we had such beautiful costumes and things. Of course, we -- the stars always had to furnish their own clothes, but we paid a lot of money for our clothes, you know, and the chorus girls, they had a group of chorus girls. Let me see who worked there. A child -- let me see who was there with us. Louie and there was -- I think Pete, Peaches and Duke, three dancers, three of the greatest dancers you ever saw in your life, Pete, Peaches and Duke.

And they had beautiful girls -- this child Ginger. We called her Ginger. She later married Ray Robinson -- Edna Mae Robinson, but her name wasn't Robinson, naturally, before she married him, but she was a beautiful little brown skinned thing, and she was one of the chorus girls. And who -- oh, they had so many chorus girls. I don't remember.

Let me get back to this. I must tell you this. The show -- the first show that I was in in New -- on Broadway -- we played Stamford, Connecticut -- was -- what was the name of that show? Wait now. I wonder -- didn't want to forget, because the first time they ever had colored showgirls, you
know, the tall girls that carry clothes. That's the show that Lena Horne's mother was in with me.
Wait now. What was the name? Dumb Luck.
Dumb Luck.
Dumb Luck with Moss and Frye. I know you've heard of them. They were comedians. Moss was a straight man, and Frye was a comedian, and they were the biggest things in America at that time, comedians.
Now, this was before How Come?
Before, yes, this was before anything. That was the first Broadway show.
Do you remember what year that was?
Dumb Luck. Let me see. I was in Chicago. Came to -- oh, --
Because I think How Come was around 1921, wasn't it, 1920 or '21?
How Come?
Yeah, wasn't it that early?
No. How Come, I think, was in '34, wasn't it?
No. No, no.
It wasn't?
How Come was --
I'm going to call Eddie Hunter and ask him.
I mentioned it in my Bessie book.
You did?
And I'll find -- you don't have to call Eddye I'll find it here.
And mentioning Connie's Inn, they had a violinist there named Allie Ross. Oh, he was marvelous.

How Come opened at the Attucks Theater in Norfolk, Virginia, which is now the Booker T. Theater, January 15th, 1923. It played between there and Washington, D. C., and Philadelphia for the next few weeks. Bessie joined it in January -- January 29th of '23, and it played at the Dunbar in Philadelphia.
I did. Uh-huh. Yeah.
You know, so it probably must have been -- because Bessie wasn't with it very long.
No.
So it must have been 1923.

Oh, yeah, uh-huh. Well, this was way -- Now, listen -- another thing. What did I see -- oh, let me see whether I -- I think I've got something here that'll help you out too, Chris. Oh, Lord, all this rattling on there.
Oh, that's all right?
You sure?
Uh-huh, as long as you're not talking while it's on.
Let's see. (inaudible) 19 -- (inaudible) attend school work and outside music. 1912 to -13 I worked at Dago Frank's.
In Chicago.

Yes. '14 to '16 I was -- Hugh Hoskins. '17 into the early '20's it was the Panama, the Deluxe, the Paradise Gardens, Tony Jackson at the Elite I told you about Elite Number Two. The Peek Inn, the Lorraine Gardens and the Dreamland.
All in Chicago.
Yeah, 1917 to '20's. Now, recorded with Fletcher Henderson in '21 for the Black Swan Label.
Right.
All right. Is this holding up -- holding you up?
No, go ahead.
Uh-huh. '22 -- Paramount label, New York. See? '23 in How Come -- you got it right. Uh-huh, at the Parlor Theater.
That was right.
Louie Armstrong -- and 1924 Louie Gennett Armstrong and I recorded for Jeannette label. You got that?
Uh-huh, yes.
'25 and '26 for Okeh, me (inaudible).
And '24, that's when you recorded with Josephine Baker, Beauty
Yes. '26 at the Coliseum, Chicago. '26, Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace.
Yeah. Now, did you sing with Earl Hines?
Well, not just --
Or opposite him or what?
Well, he -- his band was at the Grand Terrace when I worked there.
I see.
I wasn't a -- I've never been a band singer. See?
Uh-huh. Did you ever have your own pianist?

Yes. I had my own pianist. I had my own pianist; a girl named Laura played for me out in vaudeville when I was playing the big white houses, Laura. And I had a boy dance with me named Leroy Bloomfield.
I see.
See? That was when I played the big white houses here in New York. See? Maybe I can come to that. Let me see. Coliseum -- recorded Victor label in Camden, New Jersey, in '27.
Yes. Now, I have all of your recordings.
Oh, you've got all of them.
Yes.
Now, '28 was at Chez Florence in Paris. '28 -- Palladium in London, six weeks. '28 was Robeson, Edith Day in Showboat at Drury Lane.
Right. That was '28?
Yes.
I thought that was -- it went into '29.
That's right. '29 was Columbia records. You got that?
All the records, I have.
Oh, you got all the records. Wait a minute.
That's when you did 'My Particular Man' and all that.
And then in '52 I went --
This is what -- this is the information Sheldon Harris has gotten together?
Yes. Yeah, for me. Now, I tell you what. You know, started with --
Some of that he got from me.
He did? Showboat -- I mean not Showboat, but I started with the first USO show. I took the
first colored unit to tour the China-Burma-India theater, the beginning of the war.
Yes, that we'll get to later.
Oh, all right. Okay, come back.
You're still in the '30s.
Well, still in the '30's?

Well, still, when I go back to the '20's and talk about Chicago during that period, because I remember years ago Lil telling me a great deal, and I remember sitting with you and Lil, you know, and you two were talking.
Yes. Well, tell me about it, and then I can get -- come back to you.
Well, I thought some of the clubs -- now, you described to me -- you described to me the Dreamland. And that's the one that had the glass door and everything. And that was the --
The nightclub.
-- most swank --
Yes, that's right.
-- club there.
That's right.
Which one would you rank second after that?
Second? I think the Grand Terrace would be second.
Uh-huh. That was upstairs, wasn't it?
No, the Grand Terrace was further over, 35th --
No, I don't mean upstairs from the Dreamland. I mean was it on the 2nd floor?
No.
It was on the ground floor?
Uh-huh. All of them were on the ground floor with the exception of Dreamland. I don't remember.
That had two floors.
Let me see, the Panama had two floors, but Panama, it was just a little club. Of course, it was lovely, but I mean it wasn't -- nothing fancy like the Dreamland.
Uh-huh. Now, wasn't Florence Mills -- wasn't she in Chicago during that time in one of the -- with the --
She's the one, I told you. It was Brick Top, Nettie -- Nettie Compton, pianist -- Mattie Hite --
Wasn't Twinkle --
No, she was with me. Let's see. Florence Mills, Brick Top, Cora Green -- Cora Green -- Nettie Compton --
Mattie Hite.
-- Mattie Hite. That was Brick -- downstairs was Florence Mills.
Now, also around the period singing in Chicago was Ollie Powers.
Sang with me at the Dreamland. He's the one.
Uh-huh. Tell me about Ollie Powers.

Oh, Chris, he was wonderful. Great big, fat guy about your color. Looked like an ofay boy, fat and had the most wonderful disposition you ever saw in your life and just as sweet as he could be. And what a voice! He's the one that I heard sing 'After All These Years', and, Chris, when he got through singing, it was it. And the women used to come in there just to hear Ollie sing 'After All These Years.' The ones that were broken hearted had trouble, you know, [manita?] trouble, domestic troubles. They'd come in to hear Ollie sing 'After All These Years.' 'Don't Say You Don't Want Me.' Did you ever hear it?
Yes, I heard you sing it. You recorded it for me.
Yeah, but I didn't record it good like Ollie. Oh, he was marvelous. I wish I could make a record, make that thing again.
He had a very strong voice.
Oh, yes. No, we -- none of us had --

Florence Mills was the only one that -- that you could hear without -- and didn't have a mike, but still you could hear her. But we could -- we didn't have a mike, and you could hear -- you could hear us to 145th Street. Sometimes we'd have to kind of soften up. Oh, Lord, we'd have to soften up a little bit because we'd be singing so loud. No mike, no such thing.
Even when they brought a mike to me, I'd say, I don't want that thing. You know? Don't bring me no mike.
And what about Mattie Hite?
