Freddie Keppard?
Yes.

I never had much dealings with him, but he always seemed to be a very nice fellow, but he seemed to stay to himself more or less. I don't remember having very much to do with him, because as I say, he -- I used to say, 'Hello, Freddy,' and keep going. One of those things. I never had much to say to him.
Do you remember George Mitchell?
Yeah.
Another trumpet player.
Tall, skinny fellow.
Was he? I don't know. But he used to play with Jellyroll. Later on, in the '20s, he played with Jellyroll Morton.
You know, I worked with Jellyroll, too.
Yes, I know. I wanted to ask you about that.
You're coming to that.
Yes.
Uh-huh. I don't -- George Mitchell. Maybe it'll come to me, but I can't recall right now. But anyhow, now we're going from the De Luxe.
Yes. We haven't really -- well, we were talking about the Elite Number One and the Number Two.
Uh-huh.
What was the difference between those two?

The Elite Number One was way downtown -- I mean, not way downtown. It was down around a hundred and -- it was further down on State Street than Elite Number Two. I don't know why they called it Elite Number Two. I don't know why Mr. Jones, Tenan Jones, named it --
Maybe it's like the 81 Theaters.

Maybe so. Maybe so. But I know he had a brother named Give-a-Damm Jones, you know, and he was -- yeah, he was -- I don't know. The cop told him something, and he told him he didn't give a damn. I don't know what it was, but that's the story about Give-a-Damn. But anyhow, now we're going from the De Luxe, aren't we?
Yes. You haven't described the De Luxe. You said there was a billiard parlor downstairs.
Yeah. Well, of course I used to just go upstairs and do my work and come on downstairs. I was
never much of a -- I didn't drink.
Uh-huh.

I didn't smoke. And I didn't socialize much. I always -- they used to call me and say I was swell headed, and I thought I was better than the rest of the entertainers, because I didn't sit around in bars and things. I just -- I was reared by an old, old, old lady, what rearing I had, when I was at home. And I was always told by my grandmother, and my mother, to be a lady, always respect yourself and you can demand respect. So I was always to myself.
Well, you obviously didn't forget that.
Huh?
You obviously did not forget that.
Oh, thank you. More or less I stayed to myself.
But now, I was going to ask you that also. Now, you were very young and you were in Chicago without your family.
Yes.
You ran away from home. So where did you live? Did you have an apartment?
No. Not here. When I got off -- I told you about my school teacher giving me the pass?
Yes.
Did I tell you all of that?
Yes.

Her name was Miss Florida Edgerton. Florida Cummings was her name. I didn't know her name was Edgerton till later years. And I didn't know that the gentleman that was beside her was her husband, you know. But I know that I got on with the lady and the gentleman. The school teacher, my school teacher was the one I was interested in. And I got off the streetcar -- Lord, have mercy. Sometimes I think about that. I got off the streetcar and left them on the streetcar, but when I got off, like I'm -- I was facing this way when I got off, and there was a big building called the Burlington Building. I'll never forget it. And I wandered up some steps, and there was a lady washing, and I asked this lady if she knew a girl by the name of Ellen Winston. See, I had known that there was a girl in Chicago by the name of Ellen Winston. Her mother and my mother were friends. But I didn't know where she lived. But being young and not knowing, I thought if she was in Chicago, anyplace in Chicago would be all right. I could go anyplace in Chicago and people would know where she was. So this lady was washing. I asked her if she knew a girl by the name of Ellen Winston. And she said, 'No, I don't know anybody by the name of Ellen Winston, but there's a girl that lives here by the name of Helen Winston.' She had changed her name, see? To Helen. And she says, 'This

is her Sunday off." And I said, "Well, will you please, ma'am, let me stay here till she comes?" And she said yes. And she said, "Honey, what are you doing here? Where are you from?" And I said, "Well, --" I told her I was from Memphis, you know, and she said, "You are? Does your mother know where you are?" And I said, "No, ma'am." So she said, "Well, you just sit down," and she said, "Are you hungry," you know, and I said, "No, ma'am." I was too glad that that was where Helen lived, you know. So I sat there, and when the girl came it was Helen. This girl that I was looking for. So she said, "Pig, what in the world are you doing here?" Because they called me Pig, you know. And I said, "I ran away from home." So she said, "How did you get here?" And I said, "Well, Miss Florida brought me on a child's pass." She had an eight year old child's pass, you see. So she said, "Well, you sit down there. Wait till I get my shoes off." I don't remember whether her feet were hurting, or whether it was snowing or what, but anyhow, I know she took her shoes off. And so she says, "Well, you just wait a minute." So she took this lady back in the back. I don't know what she said to her, but she must have asked the lady to let me stay there, you know. So evidently the lady said all right. So, but anyhow, when she went to work the next day, she put a dress, a long dress, on me. Because I had on some little red shoes, you know, and a little bitty dress. I wasn't nothing but a kid. And she put a dress a
little longer on me and took me out to Hyde Park where she was working. She was second cook out there, you know.
Uh-huh.

So she spoke to the lady, and the lady let me work, and she gave me $6.00 a week, room and board. $6.00 a week -- listen -- room and board, and said I could stay there, you know. That's room and board, $6.00 a week. And gave me the job. Peeling potatoes. Wasn't that wonderful?
Yes.

Gave me the job peeling potatoes. And so, I peeled the potatoes and stayed there, and in the meantime, I used to -- when I was -- I would sit there and hear them say that girls made $10.00 a week in nightclubs. They didn't call them nightclubs. What did they call them then? I don't know what they called them.
Cabarets?
No, they didn't call them cabarets. They called them -- I think they called them nightclubs.
Uh-huh.

And anyhow, during that time, when I was there, at night I would sneak out while Helen was working. She was tired, the second cook, you know. I'd sneak out and go down to Dago Frank's and the different places and ask them did they want to hire a girl. I didn't know you didn't say that that way. You'd say do you want a singer or something.
I'd say do you want to hire a girl. I meant did they want to hire somebody to sing, you know.
Uh-huh.

And so they'd say, "Get her out of here. My God, I'll get my license taken away from here. Get her out of here." I was so little, you know. And so they'd put me out, each place I'd go. I went to the different places where Birk and Cora Greene and the different ones were working, and they'd make fun of me. But I kept going. You know, I'm very determined. I kept going. I'd go back every night. So finally, I think I sang a song down there, down to Dago Frank's. And the man, Roy, his name was Roy, he was the manager, he said, "Bruce, get her out of here. She's terrible." So he said, "Oh, Roy, give her a chance. You can see she's nothing but a kid, so give her a chance." So he said all right, but still he didn't hire me right then. So I went back, and then in the meantime, instead of staying at Mrs. Love's, I had moved over to 32nd and Dearborn, to a lady named Miss Bern, Cora Dern. And she let me stay there. I think I paid her a dollar a week for a room. A dollar a week for this room. And I stayed there, and one night the telephone rang, and it said come down to Dago Frank's.
Uh-huh.
Come down to Dago Frank's. And I went down there and they let me start to sing. Well, in the

meantime I had heard -- you talk to me about piano again, because this is something else I want to tell you about player pianos. In the meantime, I had heard, all Night Long, 'Where the River Shannon Flows,' on this player piano, and I had heard the words from them.
Uh-huh.

See? So when I went down there I sang those two songs in high soprano, and you know as heavy as my voice is, but what did I know. And I still don't know one note from the other. So I sang all Night Long, and 'Where the River Shannon Flows.' Well, Roy scratched his head and went on back in his office, as if to say, 'Poor girl, I'll let her stay.' So they let me stay. And each day I would learn a song on that player piano.
Uh-huh.
You know? And every night, when I'd go back, I'd sing a different song I had learned off the player piano, you know?
Uh-huh.

And the girls -- they were the sporting girls, you know, and you know they are always very tender hearted, as a rule. They would give me money and then they would make me sing again, and they'd say, 'Now, don't sing it that way. Sing it such and such a way,' you know, and I would sing, and finally I made good. I stayed there a year and ten
months. That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins.
I see.
That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins. I stayed a year and ten months, because they closed Dago Frank's.
Oh. Why did they close it?
Because it was nothing but prostitutes there.
Oh. So the police closed it.
The police closed it, see? That's when I went up to Hugh Hoskins. Now, you got that?
Yes. Now, tell me how did you, during those days, how did you get new material? Did song writers or people come to you?
Yeah.
With material?

Song writers would come to me, and in the meantime I wrote a whole lot of different songs myself. And a lot of those songs that Lovey had, I was in on them, but I didn't claim anything on them because she was so good about having my "Downhearted Blues" copy written and all, and was so honest about it, you know. And then I wasn't money crazy anyway. I just thought to make an honest living was the best thing to do, you know.
Uh-huh.

So in the meantime I would -- different -- oh, people would come in with songs. They would come in with songs. Macio Pinkert (PHONETIC) came in with "Sweet Georgia Brown," and Mr. Handy brought in -- what do you call it now -- "Careless Love". It was "Loveless Love". He brought in "Loveless Love".
Yeah.

I introduced it. I introduced it. Brought it on a piece of brown paper like you wrap groceries in, you know? And then Porter Granger, he came in with songs like "Michigan Water Tastes Like Sherry Wine," and Mike Jackson brought in songs to me. And, well, different ones, different people.
Uh-huh.
Let me see. Sissle and Blake? No, not Sissle and Blake. Different ones would, and somebody brought in a song to me called, "I'm Going Away Just to Wear You Off My Mind".
Oh, yes.
Which I made with Eubie Blake. Well, different ones would bring songs in to me, anyhow, and that's how I got my material.
If you liked them you'd --
If I liked them I would sing them. If I didn't feel them I wouldn't sing them. I didn't care. They
used to offer me money to sing them.
Right.
But I wouldn't sing them if I didn't feel them, because I wouldn't do it just for the money. It wasn't the money that I was too interested in. However, I wanted to make a living, see.
Uh-huh.
Now, after I -- well, then from the De Luxe I went across to Dreamland, and there's where Mr. Bottoms, Bill Bottoms, who turned out to be Joe Louis's dietician, he owned the Dreamland.
Yes.

Across the street. And he used to -- he had different people out trying to get me to work for him. And I got $17.50 a week. Oh, that was money, $17.50, and there's where I really made money, because Dan Gaines and most of these fellows were gamblers, now, over to Dreamland --
Yes.
-- were the gamblers and the pimps and everybody came, white and colored.
Dreamland --
Now, there's where there was decoration.
Yeah. That's the one I had a picture of.
Yeah. Had the big --
With the balcony and the bandstand.
That's where Lil and them sat up on the balcony.
Right.
And under the balcony were tables, too, and then there was a big square glass and the dance floor.
Uh-huh.
See? And that's where -- and I think Mr. Bottoms and them were the first ones to start having the breakfast dances.
Uh-huh.
See, you'd start -- people would come in for breakfast dances. Excuse me. And then --
At Dreamland you had a mixed clientele.
Oh, very much so.
Uh-huh.
Very much so, black and white. Now that was where --
Did you have the pickpockets and that element there?
Everybody came, but it wasn't exclusively the pickpockets and the sporting people.
Uh-huh.
But they came and the pickpockets didn't bother anybody. They came to enjoy themselves, and they did.

They didn't bother anybody. They didn't pick anybody's pocket or anything like that. It was all types of people, and some of our elite, the Chicago elite, came, too. They used to -- oh, and talk about smart. Now, there's where I started putting on clothes.
Uh-huh.

Had to dress. And a friend of mine, Carrie Ward, Carrie Mae Ward, she was a friend of mine and she was crazy about good clothes. And she used to go downtown and pick out the smartest clothes. I was the first one started wearing -- you know, like the Turks wear, like the big bloomers at the legs, like the --
Oh, yes.
I was the first one to wear those kind of clothes.
Now, we are now talking about -- when you were at Dreamland, what year are we talking about?
The year of Dreamland?
It was before --
Well, that was before I came to New York.
Yes. So we're still not in the '20s yet.
No. Uh-huh. No, we're not into the '20s yet.
We're getting close to it, right.

Getting very close to it, though, because when I -- when I -- while I was working at Dreamland I worked at the -- I mean, when I left Dreamland I worked at a little old club over there on Wabash. No, I don't want to bring that, because that's when I left and came right straight to New York. I worked at Dreamland, and I used to work down at the after hours clubs, too. I used to double down to the after hours clubs, to the Eden and those clubs.
Oh, yes.
Make money down there.
Did they serve food at the Dreamland?
Yes, oh, yes. Mr. Bottoms, he was a cook himself, you see. As I say, he was Joe Louis's dietician.
Right.
And the food, everything, was first class at Dreamland.
Uh-huh.
And they had to be first class. They had a guy at the door, old Jones at the door, yelling ladies and gentlemen there. And I worked with a fellow named Ollie Powers. What a voice.
He had a very high voice.
Tenor.

Yes. But what a tenor. He had one of the sweetest tenor voices you ever heard in your life. And they had a girl there named Bertha Hill, I think her name was. She had a sweet voice. Then you had May Alex She's another one used to run and do the split.
She worked with Jimmy Noone a lot.
Yeah. She worked with Jimmy Noone a lot.
Uh-huh.
May Alex You know how she got that job? She worked at the stockyards.
Uh-huh.

And she used to come in all the time, you know, as a customer. Well, when I got ready to leave the Dreamland, I told her, I said, "I'm going to New York and I'll ask Mr. Bottoms to leave you in my place." And that's how she got the job. Mr. Bottoms gave her the job when I left Dreamland. Now, I worked at Dreamland, and I'm trying to think if I didn't come back to Chicago and work at the Sunset. I don't think the Sunset was right along while I was just working regularly.
It was in the '20s.
Yeah. I think --
The Sunset -- the building that housed the Sunset --
Yeah.
-- was either owned or managed -- I guess it was owned by Joe Glaser's mother.
It was? I didn't know that.
And Louis was at the Sunset. That's how Louis met Joe Glaser.
Uh-huh.
Because his mother was the landlord there.
I see. Uh-huh. He was crazy about his mother. Joe Glaser.
Yes. Yes.
Oh, he adored his mother. He was a wonderful man, Chris.
Was he? I wanted to ask you about that.

I want to tell you something about Joe Glaser. Joe Glaser might have been mixed up with gangsters and he might have been a gangster himself, but he was one of the finest gentlemen. If you were a lady, Joe Glaser treated you as a lady, and Joe --
End of tape 6
Joe Glaser had one of the biggest hearts in the world. Joe Glaser gave me $100.00 every year to send to my church. Every year. And always said, 'If you want more
you can have it." He was a wonderful, kind, tender hearted man, although he was very abrupt.
Uh-huh.
Very abrupt. But he adored Louis. He loved Louis. And he loved Miss Sarah Churchill, who was his secretary.
Uh-huh.
Sarah Churchill. He was a kind, good man. In fact, can I tell you something? All those gangsters were nice fellows.
Uh-huh.

May I tell you they all had hearts. In their way they might have been cruel, but they were all very kind to people. You know, they might have the ones that they wanted to get rid of or something like that, but they were big hearted and gentlemen.
But they killed their own.

They killed their own. They were gentlemen, kind hearted, and I bet you those gangsters have given up more money to charity than anybody else. Believe me when I tell you. Now, so now we finished about Joe Glaser.
Yes.
And I went to see him until he died. And the day he died I went to the hospital, but they wouldn't let me in. I went every day that he was sick, I went to the
hospital to see him, and I would go there and just stand and look at his lying in bed and walk away. He was unconscious. He didn't know it. But I would go just the same.
Uh-huh.
And the day he died I went right to that bed, and when they were getting ready to do him up to send him down to the morgue I was standing right there. He was a good man.
Now, do you remember when you first came into contact with gangsters? When were you first aware of gangsters in the clubs?

I was first aware of gangsters in the clubs, it was at Burnham, Illinois. There was a club out there called the Burnham Inn. B-u-r-n-h-a-m, Burnham Inn. It was in Burnham, Illinois. I used to have to take a train to get out there. And when I went out -- I was working out there and making a whole lot of money, and I know that's the first time I knew that I was working with gangsters. And then I was naive again, because this fellow that -- fellow that killed somebody and got away and they finally caught him. What was his name? Charley something. I don't remember his last name. It'll come to me. But anyway, this -- at the Burnham Inn, I know, one night I was singing. I told you about that, though, didn't I?
Yes. Out at Burnham.
Yeah. When the lights went out and when they went back on the man was laying there dead.
Yes.
Uh-huh. Well, that's the first time that I really knew that I was working with gangsters.
But the gangsters generally -- my impression is that the gangsters --
You would never know they --
-- were good for the artists.
Oh.
They gave the artists a lot of money and they enjoyed them.
And protected us.
Uh-huh.
Nobody would bother us.
Uh-huh.
Nobody would bother us. And remember, ask me some more about gangsters, because when I worked in Nashville, Tennessee, ask me about that, hear?
Yeah.
Don't forget.
But gangsters also hired artists, right? They ran some of the clubs.
Some of the clubs.
Yeah.
Gangsters ran most of the clubs.
Uh-huh.
And had people fronting for them.
I see. Yeah.
See? People used their names for them. But I can't swear that they did.
Yeah.
You know, I don't know, and I'm not going to get into that.
Right.
No, because they were all -- they were so good to me that I have absolutely nothing to say about them but something good. Nothing.
Now, I just want to -- I know this is jumping in time --
Uh-huh.
-- but I want to, while we're thinking about it, ask -- this is, I guess long after you got to New York, you met Billie Holiday at the Hotcha.

Yeah. Well, I'm trying to think. A girl -- oh, Bert Williams' niece, Lottie Tyler, she told me about Billie Holiday. She said, 'There's a girl that sings at a little club here at 133rd,' and she says, 'I want you to hear her.' And I went there to hear her, and I just was so carried away with her work, you know. And I used to go in and

talk to her and ask her to sit down. I never did drink anything but lemonade or Coca-Cola or something, you know, but I don't remember Billie drinking. I think she had lemonade all the time. I don't think she drank anything. Stop picking your face. You'll pick it -- shame on you.
Okay. But she was very young then. She was a teenager, wasn't she?
Yes. Billie was young and very, very pretty.
And a little on the heavy side?
Yes, a little on the heavy side and very good looking.
Uh-huh.

She'd sing and then I'd ask her -- I'm trying to think. It wasn't 'God Blessed the Child,' because that was later. Some song Billy used to sing for me every night I'd go in there, I'd give her money to sing this particular song. But anyhow, I'd have her sing for me every night, you know. Every night when I would get off from work, I'd go right into the Hotcha to hear Billie. And then I'd go down to Baron's, down to Baron Wilkins. He had a brother named Leroy.
Yeah.
Wilkins. I'd go down to Baron's to hear -- there was a girl there, I think her name was Hannah Sylvester.
Uh-huh.
Hannah Sylvester. I would go in there to hear her sing. And then there was -- there was -- I can't think of this girl's -- what was this girl's name that sang in Baron's? Was it Ethel Waters? Yes.
Ethel Waters sang there.
Ethel Waters. It was Ethel Waters. She sang in Baron's. And there was some other girl. But anyhow, I'd go in there to hear Hannah Sylvester sing, too, because I'm still crazy about her singing.
Uh-huh.
You know.
She's still around, I think.
Yep. Yeah. She's still -- and doing fine, I understand. So then I would -- but I never missed going to Billie, every night.
Did you ever go to Monette's, Monette Moore's place?
Yeah. Monette. I think Monette sang at Baron's, didn't she, or did she?
She had a place. There was a place they called Monette's.
I never -- I don't remember going to her place.
I see. Monette Moore was singing
She was making records, too, you know.
Yes.
Yeah. And she could sing, too.
Uh-huh.
She made nice records. I liked Monette.
I liked her work so much.
What was the Hotcha like?
The Hotcha --
Do you remember singing from table to table?
-- was just a little joint. Yeah, the Hotcha was a little tiny place.
Uh-huh.
Just about like that.
That small.
Just about like that. Yeah. It had about four or five tables, or maybe five or six tables, that's all. Just a little narrow place.
Uh-huh.
That's all. But I think Billie made a lot of money in there, because people was crazy about her.
Yeah.
She was just so unusual. Billie Holiday was an unusual singer. She had a style that nobody will ever copy.
Uh-huh.

Nobody will ever be able to copy Billie Holiday, I don't care who they are. If they're going to try to do songs that Billie Holiday did, they should do them in their own way, but not try to copy Billie Holiday, because they'll never do it.
Uh-huh.
No.
I guess I'm asking if she was moving from table to table, but I guess if it was that small she couldn't move much.
Well, she'd sing a song and if somebody else would ask her to sing something she'd go and sing for them.
Uh-huh.
But usually, when you'd go in and you'd get her to the table you wouldn't let her go.
But people -- singers were doing the same thing in New York as at Chicago. In other words, going --
Just going from table to table.
-- from table to table and collecting --
Yes.
-- the tips from the customers.
Yeah, but you know, in Chicago we were slick. We'd sing really softly, like Joe Oliver and them would
play.
Yes.
So nobody could hear, and if you wanted to hear it at the next table you'd pay for it.
(Laughter)
Now, let me see. Now, I'm still at Dreamland, aren't I?
Yes.

Well, I was working -- I doubled from Dreamland over to a little club over on Wabash. And this club -- that was just a little after hour place, just go there to make the money, more or less. And I was coming out of the door -- a fellow disliked me. I don't know why. I think he -- I don't know why he disliked me. Anyhow, he disliked me because he -- as I said, they always thought I was, you know, thought I was better than anybody else, which I didn't. But anyhow, this was a swinging door, and as I was going in he was coming out, and he pushed the door real hard to hurt me. And I went right on, did my work that night, and I went right straight home, packed my trunk and left the next morning for New York. Because he looked like he had fire in his eyes. He was going to try to hurt me one way or the other. And I didn't -- oh, I think this fellow went with May Alex
Oh.
He was a friend of May Alex And because
he thought that I thought that I was better, he didn't want May Elex to talk to me or anything like that, and May was very friendly with me.
Uh-huh.
And I think that's why he kept in his heart to hurt me.
But now, what year was that? Do you remember? That you came to New York.

New York? When did I come to New York? I think that was around -- before I came to New York, Chris, -- I jumped a little. Before I had that little misunderstanding with that fellow, that door pushing, a fellow came from Cincinnati, Ohio and asked me to work at a place called Michaelson's. And I went, did a few weeks in Cincinnati, Ohio, at Michaelson's.
I see.
See?
Uh-huh.
And while I was at Michaelson's was when I met Willard Townsend and married him.
Oh.
So I think that was in -- I have it down here. I told you what year I got married.
Yes.
All right. Well, you have that, see?
But I came back from Michaelson's, back to Chicago, and that's when I went in to New York, after I worked at Michaelson's.
I see.
See?
What was your -- now, did anyone know you in New York when you came to New York? I mean, you were known in Chicago, obviously.
No.
But not in New York.
They just knew me by my records, that's all.
Oh, you had already started making records.
Oh, I had made records for Paramount.
I see.
I had made -- yes, I made records for Paramount. And I think I made records for Bennett Jeanette.
Right.
Yes.
So you weren't exactly an unknown when you --

No, I was well known, because I was in fact what you call -- well, what people call famous, from my records. Because if you know, "Downhearted Blues," my record for Paramount, was the first blues ever to sell 100 percent mechanical. They were on every phonograph label, and that's
what I told you to remind me of the player pianos, because Pete Wendel and Max Cortlander had the piano rolls with "Downhearted Blues" on it.
Yes.
See?
Did you get money out of piano rolls?
Yes.
You did.
Uh-huh.
They paid you for that.
Yeah. Yeah. And in the meantime, let me see now, there was something else I wanted to tell you. Piano rolls, Max Cortlander, and something -- wait now, let me see what it was, what it was.
Do you want to stop for a minute?

No. I want to remember this. Let me see now, in the meantime -- something else I wanted to tell you about. I made a record for Granett, made records for Paramount, made records for -- didn't I work at the Sunset then, or did I come back? I came back to the Sunset, didn't I?
Right.

Uh-huh. Wait a minute. I made records for Paramount, I made records in my baby sister's name, Josephine Beatty was her name, and I used her name, and in the meantime I got a letter from Frank Walker which I brought,

asking me to work for Columbia, see? And I couldn't work for Columbia, because I was contracted with Paramount. And he asked me in this letter how long was my contract going with Paramount, because, you know, he said Paramount is a small label and Columbia is a big label, so you know, enticing me to come over. I loved Mr. Walker. He was a prince. He was fine.
Tell me about him.

Oh, he was so fine. He -- Mr. Walker, he was just such a kind, true man, honest to goodness. I don't know. The only thing I can say, he was a wonderful man, that's all. I don't know anything else to say.
But you never worked for him in New York.
Something happened, and I think I eventually did something for Mr. Walker. Because I know when I'd record in New York I couldn't get back to Chicago fast enough, I was that crazy about Chicago.
Uh-huh.

If I'd finish recording at 2:00 o'clock, if there was a 5:00 o'clock train back to Chicago I'd get that 5:00 o'clock train back to Chicago, I was that crazy about it. But after I got to New York, then Chicago, I couldn't take it, you know?
Yes.

Yeah. Mr. Walker and -- I certainly wish I could remember the man's name -- Felix something -- that made my records when I would go to New York to record on that wax. He would take such interest and such pains with me to see that my records were right, you know. And he would even ruin good wax to play it over to see if I was doing all right, you know, in order for me to make a good record. And my record was the first record ever to sell 100 percent mechanical. It was on every phonograph label and piano rolls, and I got nothing. I think I got $380.00 or $360.00 once, who Mr. Supper -- Mr. Supper, who was a good, kind man, but old Mayo Williams was the one who was cheating me out of my money and trying to get Mr. Supper to cheat me, too. Eventually I think he got him over on his side and did mean things. But Mr. Supper was a good man and didn't want to do it, you know. Mayo Williams was the one, and he's paying for it, too.
But you must be getting money now on 'Downhearted Blues'.
Oh, do you know what I got the other day?
No.
I hope I brought it. I got money from Finland --
Oh, yes.
-- from Denmark, from Finland. I have
it here. I'll show it to you.
Uh-huh.
Royalties on 'Downhearted Blues'. Now, what are you going to do about that? Isn't that wonderful?
Yes.

I'm still getting money. But the contract, just think, I got a fourth of a penny. I was supposed to get a fourth of a penny on the record and I didn't get that. Isn't that unkind? You know, fate's a -- but I'm living to tell it. That's the part I'm proud of.
Right.
God is so good. He's good. I'm living to tell how I was cheated, and still getting contracts sent to me to sign away my rights, my rights and all.
Yes.
But ASCAP and AGAC have done some wonderful things. They fixed it so you not only get your 75 years, but you get life.
Right.
And some of the contracts that we have signed, we can recall them and resign them in our way. God is so good. Yes.
It's about time, I guess.
About time. And I'm living to tell it. I'm living to tell it. That's right, I'm living to tell it.

My grandmother always told me, keep God in front of you. You'll make it. Uh-huh. I'm living to tell it. Send me contracts now to sign, and they take your material, you have your material with a certain publisher, and he'll take all your material and turn it over to somebody else without your signing the fact that you want your stuff to go to that particular person or particular organization or company. Take advantage of you. All right. That's all right. I'm living to tell it.
That's good.
Yes. And maybe that'll help somebody else that don't know what they're doing.
Of course.
Now, you want -- what else?
Yes. Do you want to stop just a second?
Did I put in -- yeah, you want to stop a little while, don't you, honey? All right. Yeah. Yeah, baby. Yes, darling.
We'll think about things to go into.
Yeah. Now, and that was -- that was -- what year was that?
We were just talking --
I know I married in -- you've got the year down, so you know what year that --
I wanted to read this letter you brought.
Help yourself.

Into the tape. It's from the Columbia Graphophone Company, 1819 Broadway, New York City, recording studios, dated January 19th, 1923, addressed to Miss Alberta Hunter, number 64 East 36th Place, Chicago, Illinois. "Dear Miss Hunter. Replying to your letter of the 15th instant, won't you please advise me at your earliest convenience just how long your exclusive contract with the Paramount Company runs. No doubt you know that the Paramount Company is very small indeed, and the prestige that you gain from singing for them is very limited. Regarding Joe Oliver's band, my only idea in this respect was to use them as an accompaniment for you in case you did work for us. It will therefore be necessary for us to forget them until such a time as you will be ready to do a test record for us. We will try to see what can be worked out of the "Downhearted Blues" for you. In the meantime I would ask that you let us know about the Paramount contract as soon as possible, so we can make our plans accordingly. With kind regards we remain very truly yours," and signed Frank B. Walker, Columbia Graphophone Company.
Now, you had apparently written them a letter about "Downhearted Blues".

He wrote me a letter first and I answered his letter. I don't remember what it was about, but he wrote me a letter first and I was answering his letter and in the meantime I mentioned something to him about "Downhearted Blues". That's how "Downhearted Blues" happened to be mentioned in his letter.
It's interesting. This is a letter going from New York to Chicago and it has a two cent stamp on it.
Isn't it interesting how times have changed.
(Laughter)
Isn't that something? Isn't that something? Two cents. That's right, from New York to Chicago. Now we pay 13 cents, don't we, now?
Yeah.
13 cents. And if you send a special delivery letter they don't send it special. They just send it along with the ordinary mail.
And in those days I think we had, up till recently, two deliveries a day.
Oh, absolutely. Absolutely.
So everything deteriorates.
Oh, everything, yeah. Now, Mr. --
So you never did record at that time
for Columbia.
At that particular time, no, not for Columbia.
And you apparently wanted Joe Oliver to accompany you?
Yeah. I wanted Joe Oliver to accompany me, because I was crazy about his work, and I knew if I had -- we didn't bother about arrangements at that time, you know.
Uh-huh.

Because if I started a song, you know, they'd just play what I -- you know, it looked like they would just feel what I wanted to do, you know, and just follow me along. We didn't bother with arrangements.
Right. Of course none of them could read music.
The majority of them couldn't.
No. And you couldn't, could you?

I still can't. I don't know one note from the other. You know how I get my music? I might be -- for instance, in the mornings, around 3:00 and 4:00 o'clock, see, I might have an idea, and lyrics will come to me. Isn't that funny? And the tune will come right along with it. And I'll get up early and go downtown and have somebody take the music down and put the words with it, the lyrics with it.
You never played piano or any
instrument.

No. I never played anything. When I was a kid I used to take one finger, this finger, and just hit down on the piano to hit whatever note -- if I'd hit one note and that wasn't the one I wanted I'd hit the next one, you know, until I'd get the one I wanted, you know. That's how I got "Downhearted Blues".
Tell me about women back in those days, the early days. Women musicians. Now, I know there was Lovey, you know, and there were quite a few pianists.
Uh-huh.
(Gonzouin) I don't know if you know Bertha Gonzouin, she's someone Lil mentioned.
(Inaudible) -- she played with Oliver for awhile, while Lil -- yeah, she played --
Must have been after I left or something.
Yeah, probably.
Oh, there was a woman named Marie Lucas. Marie Lucas. There was a woman named Marie Lucas. Real tall. Ugliest woman on earth.
I see.
She played --
I thought that was Ma Rainey.
No, Marie Lucas had her some, because she was tall and she played -- what did Marie -- Marie played piano, trombone. She played several instruments. And she was
a musician out of this world. And very few of them ever bothered with notes, you know.
Wasn't there a trumpet player, a woman named Dolly?
Yeah, Dolly. Dolly played with Ethel Waters. Dolly. She was marvelous. And one of my musicians that went overseas with me on my USO tours, a little girl named Jean Starr.
Jean Starr.
A little girl named Jean Starr.
What did she play?
She played trumpet, and could play trumpet, too. I mean she could really play trumpet.
So did Valeida Snow.
Valeida Snow. Oh, Valeida was wonderful. Valeida had so much soul. You know, Valeida -- now, all these women could play.
Yeah.
They could really play. But looked like Valeida would sing a song with her trumpet. She was marvelous. Valeida was a good musician, too, you know. She was a very good musician, yeah.
Yeah.
I think Valeida played the trumpet. Valeida had a sister named Laveida.
Oh, she did.
Yeah.
They just reversed it.
Yeah. Uh-huh.
Did she play also?
No, I don't think so. No, she didn't play.
I remember I used to have a record by Valeida.
Yes.
Called 'I Can't Dance, I've Got Ants in My Pants'.
Yes. Uh-huh, Valeida played trumpet.
She came to Europe.
Yes she did, and made good in Europe. She did well.
Now we were talking about -- we didn't get into -- you did a lot of work for the USO, In the CBI -- China, Burma --
India. Yeah. China, Burma, India. That was my first tour for USO. And Dick Campbell sent me. He was the one that -- you know, the getting together of the talent for USO, you know, the colored talent.
This was when, World War II?
Yeah, the beginning of World War II.
And I took the first --
After Pearl Harbor.
Well no, I was over there on Pearl Harbor. I don't know. Yeah, because I know we -- I've got pictures. Did I show you the pictures, me in Pearl Harbor?
A long time ago you showed me --

Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah. I'm trying to think, because they sent us over just after -- when the war was just declared. How did I get over there on Pearl Harbor? I guess World War II, the beginning of World War II, yes. Because --
You were with the three --

The three -- it was my unit, because I was the manager of the unit. They made me manager of each one of my units. I was the business manager for them. I paid the salaries and everything. They'd send me the money and I'd pay them and all. Advance some money if they wanted money and all. So that was the Three Rhythm Rascals. Arlie Crawford on guitar, Al Elkins on bass, and I cannot think of Leonard's name, he was on piano. They were the musicians, the Three Rhythm Rascals. We went all through China, Burma and India. That's the first unit, Rhythm and the Blues.
The next unit, they came back, they sent me out, the ETO. That was the European Theater of Operations. Went all through France and England and Germany and all those places.

And that's when I did the command performance for General Eisenhower. They sent a plane to Nancy, France and took me to Frankfurt, Germany, to the command headquarters, where Marshall Zukov presented General Eisenhower with a medal, you know, and Field Marshall Montgomery was there. He was one of the people. And I didn't know, you know, I've always had a lot of nerve. I went up and asked all of them for their autographs. I have all their autographs. Yeah. And we played all through the European theater, and I came back. I first got a medal -- a ribbon, for ETO, because that was during all the danger, you know. Because over in India, you know, the Indians, I don't know how they would get the sound, but they would get the sound long before we would get the siren sound, and they'd start running. Well, when they'd start running, we'd start running, too, you know. We'd put our washbasins over our heads and run, which was dangerous, because if ever one of those things hit that tin washbasin, you know. So anyhow, they gave us ribbons for services, you know.
Uh-huh.
And --
So you've been decorated.

Yeah. And also the Navy. I have a thing from the Navy, too, yeah. So then after we came back from CBI we went to ETO, and that's where I said Marshall Zukov presented a medal to General Eisenhower. Then we came back
and went all through the South Pacific, all through Japan and all over the -- let me see, Korea, all up across the 38th Parallel, all up that way.
So you've really been around.
Well, for 12 years I was with USO.
That long.
Yes. From the beginning of World War II to the end of the Korean War.
Whom did you work with that we might know?
Well, let me see.
Snub Mosely, I know, at one point.
Well, Snub Mosely was the last one. I was the only woman, though, with Snub Mosely.
Yeah.

With 17 men, because they said they didn't want no cry babies, and I had a lot of nerve. My bunk was (Unintelligible) -- near Russia, you know. And then Snub Mosely and all of them were working with their hats and their gloves and things on. That's the reason I've got this arthritis, I believe, because you see, I know men over there in those camps didn't want to see no woman come out there with no jeans and pants and things on, so I had -- well, I was supposed to look pretty decent, in a dress, so I had those slinky dresses, and I had nothing on but the dress, see?
Uh-huh.

Even in that cold weather. So they told me in later years I was going to feel it. Walter Winchell wrote a beautiful article and so did Dorothy Kilgallen, about me working in those thin dresses, and no coat or anything around me. And the men with their gloves and things on. And I didn't even catch cold. Never caught cold. But now I am. I'm suffering from it, you see, now. And then, after having gone through ETO and the South Pacific, then I did Stateside. I played all around here, all around the states, you know, all around, Chicago, Kansas City. Even played out here at Riker's Island.
Oh, you did?
Yeah.
Do you remember the first time you used a microphone?
Let me see.
When you first started there were no microphones.

No, I didn't use a mike overseas. I didn't use microphones. Let me see, the first place I used a microphone -- let me see, where was it? The Japanese were up high, looking down on us, and we were down below, and I was trying to sing so they could hear me too, you know, and they put one of those round kind of mikes, kind of like a dome. The ones they started using just before these that they're
Oh, yes.

Well, them. And I think that's the first time I started using a mike. Because first of all, you see, I moved around too much for a mike. I used to cover -- I didn't just stand in front. What are those soldiers going to do on the side?
But do you think that when you started, if they had had mikes and p.a. systems in those days, would that have --
Taken something from me.
-- would your style have been different then?
Oh, I think so.
You must have had to project so much.
I don't think I would have used it.
You have a very powerful voice.
Oh, thanks.
Even in 1961 when (Unintelligible). we made those albums,
Yeah.
You had such a powerful voice. I was just wondering, because a lot of singers nowadays, you hear them, they sound big on records.
Yeah, but that's that --
If you're in the studio with them, you see their mouth moving, but you can't even hear them. (Unintelligible) -- it's all microphones.
No. No.
I was just wondering, that it must have affected your style.
It would have, but I wouldn't use a mike. And then the couple or few times I did use it, I was just cramped up so that I had to get away from it. I just put the mike aside.
I'm sure a lot of singers, our singers today --
Yeah.
-- would never have made it back in those days.

No. That's the truth. That's the truth. A lot of them. Because I know several of the girls, right now, they would never have made it, and they're big timers now, but they never would have made it in those days, you know. And then, another thing, Chris, a lot of the things that they're calling blues are not blues that they're singing now, and these people, type of blues singers, they're not blues singers.
Right.
These people don't know blues, do they? You know, when we were singing the blues, for instance, if I

felt down, you know, maybe troubled, and I had it all my days, I'm telling you about it. These people -- first of all, if they would say what they are trying to say, if they would say it out loud, it's not blues. You know, they don't know blues.
You know, Alberta, you're a religious woman, and you know, I've met quite a few performers.
Yeah.
Who turned to religion in later life.
Yeah.
And very often the religious people look on the blues as sort of a sinful music. You know, Lil's mother, for instance.
I know, yeah.
But you don't seem to look on the blues as anything sinful.
Well, blues aren't sinful. You're telling a story.
Right.

Blues aren't sinful. Blues is a song from your soul. When you're singing the blues, you're singing -- the singers, as Mahalia, who was one of the greatest on earth, was singing a spiritual about some day my time will come, when she's singing that. When I'm singing, "Trouble, trouble, I've had it all my days," I'm feeling that I've had it
so long maybe some day my trouble will pass away.
What about when you were singing "My Particular Man, my handy man," what about those?
When I was singing them I was singing what I meant, but what the song meant. You understand? And I was singing it as it should be sung, I thought.
They were a little naughty.
They were a little naughty, and my mother didn't approve of that, you know.
Uh-huh.

Oh, no. My mother was a little against that. And then when I would sing "My Particular Man," I was singing that for J.C. Johnson, and I tried to do a good job, so inasmuch as the song was being sung, I wanted to sing it so that he could make the money.
Uh-huh.
You understand?
Yes.

I wanted to sing it as it should be sung, so if the record came out he could make the money. But it wasn't the type song that I really wanted to sing. Although I have sung several of the songs that were a little naughty.
Yes.
You know?
I've heard a few.
Yes, I've sung some of them. But they
weren't what I'd call blues. They were just suggestive. We called them suggestive. We didn't call them risqué.
Yes. Yes.
We called them suggestive songs. See, now, sometimes maybe in a nightclub I'd sing them.
Yes.
You know? But I was singing them because I could make the money from singing them.
When did the time come when you stopped singing? Did you just suddenly say, 'I'm through singing'?

Yes. When the time came I did well. When I finished with Snub Mosely, I did well the whole time I was in show business, fortunately. I went as far as you could go. I played Broadway. I played the Royal Theater in London. I played the Casino de Paris in Paris and the National in Copenhagen, and the places that were considered the greatest, and I figured I had gone to the top. And my records sold in the millions. So I figured I had gone as far as I could go. And I didn't -- I decided I wasn't going to sing anymore because I didn't want to spoil what I had done. People would come to me and say -- want me to go in a show, and I didn't feel I could do, maybe, justice to what they wanted me to do. And I -- inasmuch as I had made good, I wanted people to remember me --
As you --
-- as I was.
Yes.

On top. I didn't want them to say, "Is she still here?" I didn't want that. So, when my mother passed, on January the 17th, 1954, I went to -- started to school the next day, nursing school. I went to the YWCA nursing school on 137th Street, and Phyllis Butts, that was the instructor there, and she accepted me. And I started to school, nursing school. And I was a little old there, you know, but fortunately I left that state board with a marvelous rating.
Uh-huh.

Yes, I did. And some of the girls who were taking the psychometric test, they couldn't pass it. They flunked it, and they had just come out of high school. And when we were doing the problems on narcotics, I hope to tell you, Miss Southern who was the instructor, had me to get up and work the examples on the narcotics, to show them how they should be done. All right, now.
So --
And I was the oldest one.
And that's when you stopped singing.
So then, when we did those albums
together in '61 --
Now, wait a minute. '54. '54. Then Mrs. Patterson came along. Well, that was an acting part. It wasn't singing.
Uh-huh.
It was acting. And then Inger Stevens came along, with "Debut".
What was that?
That was a show opened on Broadway.
Yeah?
Didn't last long, because the fellow -- I think there was a little jealousy there between -- performers get jealous of one another, and their acting and billing and all, you know.
Uh-huh.
So that didn't last long. Inger Stevens. You remember Inger Stevens.
Yes.
"The Farmer's Daughter". She was a lovely girl. Oh, she was so lovely. And so then I -- after those shows -- oh, I'm ahead of my story. "Mamba's Daughters".
That's right.
'39 and '40, at the Empire.
We've already talked about that.
Have we? Oh, all right.
I just wanted to know when you
stopped singing.
Oh. I definitely stopped singing in '54. '54.
You know, it's remarkable how well you did in '61 when we made those albums. You would not think you had stopped singing.
Well, I tell you what, Chris. Do you know I never sing?
No?

Never. I never even sing. I never even hum. Isn't that funny? But you know what, I never abused my voice. I've always gotten rest. I don't drink or smoke and never did. So I always preserved my health. Now, I can blurt out now, if you want me to.
What?
Blurt out a little bit. I mean sing a song.
I'm sure you can. I'm sure you can. I know it.
Yes, Lord. And I've had so many offers to go in shows and to do TV. Do you remember, that ABC wanted me to be interviewed, you know?
Right.
And the different ones. But I don't know why. I just stopped singing.
Well, I always thought that one reason you didn't want to do TV interviews was because you were --
And I don't like to dress up.
-- hiding the fact that -- you know, that you didn't want people to know --
How old I was.
-- how old you were at the hospital. I always thought well, she didn't want them to see her.
(Laughter)
That's the truth. You sure did guess it.
Uh-huh.

And then another thing, Chris, I had to dress up so much in show business. I had to spend so much money for clothes. And a lot of these girls that have these smart shops on Madison Avenue and in the different big stores, I got my clothes strictly from them. And then Patou dressed me in Paris, you know.
Yes.
See? And I had to dress up so much that I detest clothes. I want to always be neat and passable.
And comfortable.
Comfortable. And having to put on -- God knows I love him. I love God because he's been so good to

me. And still is. The reason -- one of the main reasons I don't go to church, I've got to put on a hat. I don't like hats. And I don't like -- I'll have to dress up a little to go to church. I don't want to wear my jeans to church, although people do wear jeans. But I don't want to put on jeans to go to church, so I stay away from church. And I have a little radio, and on WHN, tuned to WHN, and the only time I turn that radio on is say I start about 6:00 o'clock on Sunday morning, to listen to the services, and there's Dr. Oswald Hoffman comes on at 8:30, and I listen to him. But I leave that thing on from about, say about 6:00 o'clock, until all the religious services go off, and then I turn that radio off. I don't turn it on again until the next Sunday, at 6:00 o'clock, see, when I hear my services.
You don't even listen to music on the radio.
Well, I put my radio -- I have a Magnavox that I put on to listen to the news and other music.
Uh-huh.
But I leave that one on.
Do you watch television?
Once in awhile. I watch television for the news. Now, I like Red Foxx, and I like --
Do you like Aunt --
What's that guy's name that -- huh?
Do you like Aunt -- the Aunt in
Sanford and Son.

Oh, yeah, I think she's adorable. She's adorable. And I like -- I like Sammy, but I'm mad with Sammy because I've written him several letters and he didn't answer. And I know Sammy so well, he shouldn't put on the ritz with me, because I know him so well, see. And Billy Eckstine. I'm crazy to get in touch with him. I sent him a letter and sent it registered special and requested a return letter.
Well, I'm going to help you with that.

And he didn't -- and the letter came back just as it was. Now, sometimes they think you're begging, but I don't need anything from anybody, because I have preserved my health and I have saved my money, so I don't need any favors from anybody. I'm only trying to get in touch with Billy Eckstine because I would like to hear that song of his, 'If I Can Help Somebody'. That I'm always trying to do, as you know.
Uh-huh.

And that song has helped me a lot in my work, too, see? So I don't need anything. So anytime any of them get a letter from me, they can just open it and read it, because there's no begging. Because I'm sending everybody that I can think of that needed a little help, sending them

some money. So I hope they will get that. Now, one person that always answers my letters and is as sweet to me as she can be is Lena Horne. If I write Lena Horne she'll answer me right away. And I call her mother, Mrs. Edna Horne, and talk to her all the time. She's as sweet as she can be. Because she was in my first Broadway show with me.
She was.
A show called "Dumb Luck".
Do you remember her when she was with Noble Sissle?
Who, Lena?
Lena Horne.
I remember little Lena, bless her little old pretty heart.
Leona Horne or something like that.
Leona?
I saw a picture in the --
I don't know Leona Horne.

-- Amsterdam News from the late '30s, there's a picture of her and she's got a baton in her hand, and it says, "Pretty Miss Leona Horne, fresh out of high school, conducts the Noble Sissle Orchestra."
Oh, bless her little heart. Well, I didn't know that.
"We understand she's a chirper, too."

I didn't know that. That was before me. I don't know that. Not before my time, but I don't know about that. But I want to make it plain. So anytime any of the performers get a letter from me, it's just that I'm inquiring about them because I would like to hear from them. And Will Mastin, who is the uncle of Sammy, the Will Mastin Trio?
Yes.
I would like very much to contact him and Sammy's father, because I used to go and sit in their dressing room every day while I was trying to find work, several times, you know.
Is his father still alive?
Yes.
He is?

Uh-huh. Yes. I used to go and sit in their dressing room and talk with them, and Sammy ran out on the stage when he was nothing but a kid, in Boston. We were on the same program. So anytime I write them, if they want to answer, all right, but if they don't, all right. But I want them to know I'm not begging.
Yeah.
Because I don't need anything.
Of course he may not even know that you ever wrote to him.
Well see, the thing of it is, some of them have these little fresh, smart secretaries, you know.
Yeah.

And they see Alberta, they see it's a woman, and they think it's somebody trying to get friendly with him or something, and don't answer. But I'm old enough to be his great grandmother, so they can answer, you know. Some of them have -- chances are Billy Eckstine didn't get that letter.
Yeah.
Because I sent it to Westbury, and there's no way in the world for them to say unknown, because he was working there.
That's right.
See, so how is he unknown? I was simply asking for his record.
Well, I'm going to get you the record.
Oh, I'd give anything in the world to get that record.
But have we left anything out?
Yes.
What?
Now, did you get in there about the Three Palms? They were with me.
Now, this was a group you were on a USO tour with.
Yes, uh-huh.
They were dancers.
Yeah. They had dancers. Well, the band with me was Herbie Cowan. Herbie Cowan was the drummer but it was his band. And we did -- oh, we did so well. That was on the ETO, the ETO group.
Oh, I wanted to ask you, did you ever -- were you ever performing on 52nd Street when that --
Yes.
Tell me about it.
52nd Street, La Commedia.
Uh-huh.
Mr. -- what was that man's name? Mr. Fox?
I've heard of La Commedia.
Yeah. Oh, that was one of the smart, little intimate clubs. Right across the street from Billie.
Yeah?
Yes. Right across the street from where she worked.
What was it, the Onyx, or --
Yes. The Onyx. Uh-huh. And Mr. -- no, his name wasn't Fox. Mr. Schwartz. No. I'll think of

his name, maybe, later. But it was La Commedia, and that was one of them smart little clubs, little intimate clubs. That's what we had, didn't we? Oh, Chris, we had that years ago, little smart, intimate clubs, where the people would come in and sit and talk and laugh, and no dancing or anything like that. Just an intimate little club.
Did you ever meet Mildred Bailey?
Yeah. Mildred Bailey recorded 'Downhearted Blues'.
I know she did.
Yes. Oh, she was a darling.
Uh-huh.
She could sing awhile, too.
Oh, yes.
Yes. Mildred could sing awhile. She made a lovely record of 'Downhearted Blues'.
I've heard that she was very jealous of Billie Holiday.
And that she was so jealous of Billie Holiday that, to spite her, she hired Billie's mother to be her maid.
Oh, I don't believe it.
You don't believe that?
No. I don't believe it. Mildred was
